findings.subsystem: MCP JSON-RPC protocol core (dispatch + content blocks)
findings.purpose: The pharos MCP server core is a single pure-function dispatcher that turns one inbound NDJSON line into a JSON-RPC response string (or no response for notifications). `pharos/mcp/server.gleam` parses a JSON-RPC message, classifies it as a request (has `id`) or notification (no `id`), dispatches by `method` to one of three handled methods (`initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`) plus notification handlers (`initialized`, `notifications/cancelled`), and builds spec-compliant `{jsonrpc, id, result}` / `{jsonrpc, id, error}` envelopes. `content_block.gleam` defines the unit of tool output — currently only the `text` content block variant, though the spec also allows `image` and `resource`. The MCP protocol version advertised is "2024-11-05".
findings.how_it_works:
CONTROL FLOW. The public entry point is `handle_line(pool, line) -> DispatchResult` (server.gleam:81). It calls `json.parse(line, message_decoder())`. On parse failure it returns `ProtocolError(error_response(None, -32700, "Parse error"))` — note the JSON-RPC parse-error code -32700 and a null id (None). On success it hands the decoded `Message` to `dispatch`.

MESSAGE DECODING / NOTIFICATION-vs-REQUEST. `message_decoder()` (server.gleam:95) reads `method` (required string), then `id` as an `optional_field` defaulting to `None`, then `params` as an `optional_field` defaulting to `None`. The id/notification distinction is purely structural: if `maybe_id` is `Some(id)` it produces a `RequestMessage(id, method, params)`, if `None` it produces a `NotificationMessage(method, params)`. There is no `jsonrpc: "2.0"` validation on inbound messages — only `method` is required. The `Id` type is `IntId(Int) | StringId(String)` decoded via `id_decoder()` using `decode.one_of(int, [string])`, matching the JSON-RPC spec that ids are string-or-number.

DISPATCH (the core function, server.gleam:113). `dispatch(pool, message)` pattern-matches on the Message variant:
  - RequestMessage(id, method, params): sets a logging correlation id from the request id, logs the method, then a `case method` selects: `"initialize" -> Reply(initialize_response(id))`, `"tools/list" -> Reply(tools_list_response(id))`, `"tools/call" -> Reply(handle_tool_call(pool, id, params))`, and a fallthrough `other -> Reply(error_response(Some(id), -32601, "Method not found: " <> other))`. Note: -32601 is the JSON-RPC "method not found" code. There is NO explicit `ping` handler — a `ping` request falls into the `other` branch and gets a -32601 "Method not found: ping" error.
  - NotificationMessage("initialized", _) -> NoReply (the post-initialize handshake ack; no response).
  - NotificationMessage("notifications/cancelled", params) -> logs/acts on the cancel then NoReply.
  - NotificationMessage(_, _) -> NoReply (any other notification is silently dropped, spec-correct: notifications never get responses).

DispatchResult is a three-variant type (server.gleam:71): `Reply(json)` (write this back to stdout), `NoReply` (notification, no output), `ProtocolError(json)` (malformed input, reply with a JSON-RPC error). Reply and ProtocolError both carry an already-serialized JSON string.

INITIALIZE HANDSHAKE (server.gleam:255). `initialize_response(id)` builds the result via `success_response` with an object containing: `protocolVersion` = the const "2024-11-05"; `capabilities` from `server_capabilities()` which is `{tools: {listChanged: false}}`; `serverInfo` = `{name: "pharos", version: "0.1.0"}` (from consts `server_name`/`server_version`); and an MCP-optional `instructions` string built by `build_server_instructions()`. Instructions start from a base sentence and, per ADR-029, append a list of custom URI schemes if any language in the registry declares them (generated live from the registry each handshake).

TOOLS/LIST (server.gleam:318). `tools_list_response(id)` returns `{tools: [...]}`. `allowed_tool_definitions()` holds a curated list of `(name, builder)` pairs (echo, get_diagnostics, hover, goto_definition, find_references, document_symbols, workspace_symbols, goto_type_definition, goto_implementation, signature_help, call_hierarchy_*, rename_preview, format_document, code_actions, apply_workspace_edit, inlay_hints, semantic_tokens, type_hierarchy_*, lsp_request_raw, fetch_uri_contents, find_symbol/get_symbols_overview/containing_symbol/find_referencing_symbols/edit_at_symbol from ADR-026, and memory_* from ADR-027), appends debug tools, then `list.filter_map` keeps only those whose name passes `tool_registry.is_allowed(name)` and instantiates the builder. Each builder returns a JSON object `{name, description, inputSchema}` where inputSchema is a JSON-Schema object.

TOOLS/CALL (server.gleam:795). `handle_tool_call(pool, id, params)` first peeks the requested tool name via `peek_filtered_name`: if the tool is filtered out by config it returns `error_response(Some(id), -32601, "Tool not enabled: ...")`. Otherwise it calls `dispatch_tool_call`. `decode_tool_call(params)` (server.gleam:3067) decodes the params object as `{name: string, arguments?: dynamic}` (arguments is an optional field defaulting to None). The big `case decode_tool_call(params)` matches `Ok(#("toolname", arguments))` per tool, each delegating to a per-tool `handle_*` and per-tool argument decoder. Argument decode failures yield `error_response(Some(id), -32602, "Invalid params for ...")` (-32602 = invalid params). Unknown tool names fall through to debug.dispatch or `error_response(Some(id), -32602, "Unknown tool: " <> name)`. A param-shape failure on the whole tools/call yields -32602 "Invalid tools/call params: ...".

TOOL RESULT SHAPE / SUCCESS-VS-ERROR-CONTENT. Tool outcomes do NOT use JSON-RPC errors for tool-level failures. Instead `tool_text_result(message, is_error)` (server.gleam:3094) builds the MCP CallToolResult: `{content: [<block>], isError: <bool>}`. The content array holds content blocks rendered by `content_block.to_json`. When `is_error` is True the message is also logged to stderr at Warn. Successful LSP calls return `success_response(id, fn() { tool_text_result(json_text, False) })`; tool-domain errors (e.g. SessionFailed/RequestFailed) return the same success envelope but with `tool_text_result(reason, True)` — i.e. a JSON-RPC success whose result has isError:true. JSON-RPC `error` responses are reserved for protocol-level faults (parse error, method not found, invalid params, tool not enabled).

CONTENT BLOCKS (content_block.gleam). `ContentBlock` is currently a single-variant type `Text(text: String)`. `text(value)` constructs it; `to_json` renders `{type: "text", text: value}`. The module docstring notes the MCP spec also defines `image` and `resource` variants which are not yet implemented (v0.1 emits text only).

RESPONSE / ERROR CONSTRUCTORS (server.gleam:3118-3151). `success_response(id, build_result)` -> `{jsonrpc: "2.0", id: <id_to_json>, result: <build_result()>}` serialized via `json.to_string`. Note result is built lazily through a thunk. `error_response(id: Option(Id), code, message)` -> `{jsonrpc: "2.0", id: <id_to_json or null>, error: {code, message}}`. IMPORTANT: although the JSON-RPC spec and the schema task mention an error `data` field, this implementation's `error_response` does NOT emit a `data` field — only `code` and `message`. The id is threaded as `Option(Id)`: `Some(id)` serializes the id, `None` serializes JSON null (used for parse errors where no id could be recovered). `id_to_json(id)` maps `IntId(n) -> json.int(n)` and `StringId(s) -> json.string(s)` preserving the inbound id type.

CANCELLATION (server.gleam:176). `log_cancel_notification` decodes a `requestId` (or `id`) from params (int or string), then does a two-pronged cancel: (1) LSP side — looks up the inflight LSP request and emits `$/cancelRequest`; (2) MCP-worker side — looks up the dispatcher worker pid and sends it an exit signal, then cleans up the worker table. Misses on either lookup are normal and logged. It always returns NoReply (spec says the server SHOULD NOT respond to a cancelled request).

key_files.role: MCP JSON-RPC dispatch core: parse line, classify request/notification, dispatch by method (initialize/tools/list/tools/call), build success/error envelopes, handle cancellation. Also holds all tool definitions + per-tool handlers/arg decoders.
Tool-output content block type and JSON rendering. Single Text variant; image/resource noted as future.

code_snippets.why_notable: The dispatch function itself — the menu of handled methods and notification handling. No ping handler; unknown methods get -32601.
How notification (no id) is distinguished from request (has id) at decode time — purely structural on presence of id.
The success and error envelope constructors. Note error_response emits only code+message, NO data field; id threaded as Option with null fallback.
Tool result shape: {content:[block], isError:bool}. Tool-level failures ride a JSON-RPC success with isError:true, not a JSON-RPC error.
initialize handshake result: protocolVersion 2024-11-05, capabilities {tools:{listChanged:false}}, serverInfo {name,version}, plus optional instructions.
Content block type + JSON rendering. Only text variant exists; image/resource are spec-defined but unimplemented.

design_patterns: Pure-function dispatch: handle_line is a total function String -> DispatchResult with no side effects in the happy path (LSP I/O happens inside tool handlers via the Pool). Easy to unit-test.
Three-variant DispatchResult (Reply/NoReply/ProtocolError) cleanly encodes the JSON-RPC truth that notifications produce no output and that malformed input still warrants an error frame.
Flat, explicit case-per-tool dispatch deliberately chosen (per module docstring) so the code reads as the menu the host sees, rather than a dynamic registry lookup.
Lazy result building: success_response takes a thunk fn() -> Json so the result is only constructed when an id is in hand.
Tool-domain errors vs protocol errors are separated: domain failures ride a JSON-RPC success with {isError:true} content; only parse/method/params faults use the JSON-RPC error object.
Tool filtering layered in two places: tools/list hides disallowed tools, and tools/call peeks the name to reject disallowed tools with -32601 before decoding args.
Timeout resolution stack: compiled-in default < [tool_config.<name>] < [tool_config.<name>.<lang>] < session override < explicit timeout_ms arg, resolved per call via finalize_timeout.
gotchas: No `ping` method handler — a JSON-RPC `ping` request gets -32601 'Method not found: ping'. MCP spec defines ping as optional, so this may be a compliance gap if a host expects pong.
error_response does NOT emit a JSON-RPC `data` field — only code and message. The task asks about code/message/data; data is simply not implemented here.
Inbound messages are not validated for `jsonrpc: "2.0"` — only `method` is required by the decoder. A message missing jsonrpc still dispatches.

JSON-RPC error codes used: -32700 (parse error, null id), -32601 (method not found / tool not enabled / unknown tool), -32602 (invalid params). No -32600 (invalid request) or -32603 (internal error) paths.

Tool-level failures are NOT surfaced as JSON-RPC errors; they come back as a successful response with result.isError=true and a text content block. A naive client checking only the top-level `error` key will treat tool failures as successes.
content_block only supports Text — any tool needing image/resource output must extend the ContentBlock type first.
Parse-error responses use id null; if a request had an id but failed to parse as JSON, the id is lost (null), which is spec-acceptable but means the client can't correlate the failure.
The protocol version string '2024-11-05' is hardcoded as a const and echoed back regardless of what the client requested in initialize params (no version negotiation).
findings.type_safety_notes: Gleam models this cleanly with sum types that an Elixir port would have to enforce at runtime. `Id = IntId(Int) | StringId(String)` guarantees an id is exactly one of the two JSON-RPC-legal shapes and preserves the original type on the way out (id_to_json maps back to int/string). `Message = RequestMessage(id, method, params) | NotificationMessage(method, params)` makes the request/notification distinction a type-level invariant — a request always has an id, a notification never does — so the dispatcher cannot accidentally try to reply to a notification or omit an id from a reply. `DispatchResult = Reply | NoReply | ProtocolError` forces the transport layer to handle all three outcomes exhaustively. `ContentBlock` being a closed variant means adding image/resource is a compile-time change that the exhaustive `case` in to_json forces you to handle. An Elixir port loses all of this: ids become bare terms, messages become maps where `Map.has_key?(:id)` is the only request/notification signal (and a runtime guard must enforce it), DispatchResult becomes tagged tuples like `{:reply, json} | :noreply | {:error, json}` with no exhaustiveness checking, and content blocks become maps with a `"type"` discriminator that nothing forces you to handle completely. The Option(Dynamic) params and decode.run pipeline also become runtime pattern matches / with-clauses returning {:ok, _} | {:error, _} tuples.

geex_relevance.rationale: This is a compact, well-factored, spec-pragmatic MCP JSON-RPC core: a single pure dispatch function, a clean request/notification classifier, and minimal success/error envelope builders. The shapes (Id, Message, DispatchResult, ContentBlock) are exactly the primitives any MCP server needs and they are small enough to port verbatim. The separation of protocol errors (JSON-RPC error object) from tool-domain errors (result.isError) is a correct, important pattern geex should mirror.
geex_relevance.what_to_take: Port directly: (1) the Message decoder's structural request-vs-notification rule (presence of `id`); (2) the DispatchResult three-variant return so the transport handles Reply/NoReply/ProtocolError exhaustively; (3) the success_response/error_response envelope builders with id threaded as an Option and null fallback for parse errors; (4) the JSON-RPC error code conventions (-32700 parse, -32601 method-not-found, -32602 invalid-params); (5) the tool result shape {content:[...], isError} and the rule that tool failures are successful JSON-RPC responses with isError:true; (6) the ContentBlock type with text now and image/resource as planned variants; (7) the initialize result shape {protocolVersion, capabilities:{tools:{listChanged}}, serverInfo:{name,version}, instructions}. Improvements geex should make over this reference: add a `ping` handler (return empty result), and add the optional `data` field to error_response so structured error payloads are possible. Decide whether to negotiate protocolVersion against the client's requested version rather than always echoing the hardcoded '2024-11-05'.

findings.subsystem: MCP transport layer (stdio + Streamable HTTP/SSE) and its boundary to the server core
findings.purpose: Pharos exposes a single MCP server core over two interchangeable transports — newline-delimited-JSON over stdio and Streamable HTTP (with SSE) — by funneling every inbound JSON-RPC message through one pure entry point, `server.handle_line(pool, line) -> DispatchResult`. The transport's only job is framing: read a line/body, hand the raw string to the core, and serialize the returned `Reply | NoReply | ProtocolError` back onto its wire. Both transports share the same warm `Pool` of LSP processes, so a tool call over HTTP and one over stdio hit the same cache. The HTTP side adds session identity (`Mcp-Session-Id`) and an SSE channel for future server-initiated requests; stdio adds async per-line dispatch so cancellations can be acted on mid-flight.
findings.how_it_works:
TRANSPORT ABSTRACTION / BOUNDARY. The seam is deliberately thin and stringly-typed: `pharos/mcp/server.gleam` exposes `pub fn handle_line(pool: Pool, line: String) -> DispatchResult`, where `DispatchResult = Reply(json: String) | NoReply | ProtocolError(json: String)`. handle_line does `json.parse(line, message_decoder())`; on parse failure it returns `ProtocolError(error_response(None, -32700, "Parse error"))`, on success it calls `dispatch/2`. dispatch classifies the message as `RequestMessage(id, method, params)` (has an `id`) or `NotificationMessage(method, params)` (no `id`); requests always produce `Reply(...)` (initialize / tools/list / tools/call / method-not-found), notifications always produce `NoReply`. The whole core is pure: it takes a raw string + the shared Pool handle and returns a string (or nothing). It knows nothing about stdio, HTTP, sockets, sessions, or SSE. Each transport just supplies the line and disposes of the result. Both transports obtain the same `Pool` via `pool.global()` (a persistent_term-backed Subject), which is why the warm LSP cache is shared.

STDIO FRAMING. Framing is NDJSON — one JSON-RPC message per `
`, no Content-Length headers (the module doc explicitly contrasts this with the LSP side's `lsp/framing`). `pharos/mcp/stdio.gleam` is a thin FFI veneer: `read_line()` and `write(body)` delegate to `pharos_stdin_ffi`. The actual read loop in production is NOT the synchronous `read_line/0`; it is an Erlang port owned by the `stdio_worker` actor. In `stdio_worker.start_supervised`, the initialiser calls `open_stdin_port()` (FFI `erlang:open_port({fd, 0, 0}, [in, binary, eof, {line, 65535}])`) so the OS pipe delivers `{Port, {data, {eol, Line}}}` / `{Port, eof}` tuples straight into the actor's mailbox. A `process.select_other(PortMailbox)` selector catches those raw tuples; `decode_port_event` (FFI) projects each into `PortLine(String) | PortEof | PortOther`. On `PortLine(body)`, `handle_port_event` calls `dispatch_line` and bumps an `inflight` counter; on `PortEof` it transitions to `draining`. ASYNC DISPATCH (M10): `dispatch_line` does NOT call the core inline — it `process.spawn_unlinked`s a dispatcher process that registers its pid in an ETS table (`request_workers.insert(mcp_id, pid)`, keyed by the peeked JSON-RPC `id`), runs `server.handle_line(pool, body)`, sends the result back to the worker via a `Subject(WriterMsg)` (`WriteResponse(json)` for Reply/ProtocolError, `WorkerDone` for NoReply), then deletes its ETS entry. The worker reads the next line immediately rather than blocking, which is what lets a `notifications/cancelled` arrive in time — the cancel handler in server.gleam looks up the worker pid and `process.send_exit`s it. All stdout writes funnel back through the single stdio_worker actor (the selector maps `WriterMsg` -> `Msg` via `select_map`), so concurrent dispatchers can't interleave a half-line; `Write(json) -> stdio.write(json)`.

KEEPING STDOUT CLEAN. This is the most load-bearing detail. stdout is reserved exclusively for JSON-RPC frames; all logging goes to stderr / a ring buffer / a file (see `tool_text_result` comment: 'Stdout stays reserved for JSON-RPC frames'). Critically, `stdio.write` is NOT `gleam/io.println` — it is FFI `pharos_stdin_ffi:write_line/1`, which opens a one-off raw port `erlang:open_port({fd, 1, 1}, [out, binary])`, `port_command`s `[Body, $\n]`, then `port_close`es it. The close synchronously flushes before returning. This bypasses Erlang's `:user` group leader, which under Burrito's `-noshell -mode embedded` release runtime buffers stdout and only flushes on stdin EOF — MCP hosts hold stdin open waiting for the response, so initialize would never return before the host's 30s timeout. (A cached persistent port left bytes queued indefinitely, so close-per-write is the fix.) The same `-noshell` problem motivates the raw `{fd,0,0}` line-mode stdin port instead of `:user`.

HTTP TRANSPORT (mist). `pharos/mcp/http.gleam` builds a mist listener: `mist.new(handler) |> mist.bind(bind) |> mist.port(port) |> mist.after_start(...)`. `after_start` logs the actually-bound port to stderr and writes it to an optional `port_file` so headless callers can discover an OS-assigned port (pass `port=0`). The router (`route/3`) matches method+path: `POST /mcp` (main dispatch), `POST /mcp/respond` (stubbed, returns 204 — future server-request correlation), `GET /mcp/events` (SSE), `GET /mcp` -> 405, anything else -> 404. Every entry first runs `origin_allowed` (DNS-rebind mitigation: no Origin allowed, else must prefix-match http(s)://localhost / 127.0.0.1 / [::1]). `handle_post` reads the body with `mist.read_body(req, max_body_bytes)` (4 MiB cap), UTF-8 decodes it, then `handle_session`. SESSIONS: `is_initialize(body_text)` does a fast partial parse of just the `method` field; if it's `initialize` a fresh session id is issued and echoed back in the response via `with_session_id` (`Mcp-Session-Id` header). Every non-initialize POST must carry `Mcp-Session-Id`; missing -> 400, unknown -> 400 (`sessions.validate`). On success `dispatch(pool, body_text)` calls the SAME `server.handle_line` and maps `Reply`/`ProtocolError` -> 200 application/json, `NoReply` -> 204 empty. Note the HTTP path runs handle_line inline on the mist connection process (no request_workers table, no async kill-based cancel — the cancel handler tolerates the miss).

SSE. `GET /mcp/events` (after origin + session validation) calls `mist.server_sent_events(request, initial_response, init, loop)`. `sse_init` attaches the SSE actor's own Subject to the session (`sessions.attach_sse`) and schedules a heartbeat. `sse_loop` handles `SseMsg = Push(correlation_id, body) | Heartbeat | Close`: `Push` emits a `mist.event` named `server_request` with the correlation id as the event id (this is the channel for future server-initiated requests like workspace/applyEdit, whose reply comes back on POST /mcp/respond keyed by correlation_id); `Heartbeat` emits a comment-style keep-alive every 15s (re-armed via `process.send_after` after each message); `Close`/send-failure detaches and stops. This is the only part not yet fully wired (respond is a 204 stub).

SESSIONS STATE. `pharos/mcp/sessions.gleam` is a single OTP actor wrapping `State(table: Dict(String, SessionState))`. `SessionState(last_activity_us: Int, sse_subject: Option(Subject(SseMsg)))` — that's all it tracks per session: last-activity timestamp (for idle eviction) and the optional SSE delivery Subject. Messages (opaque `Msg`): `Issue` (generate a 32-char hex id via `crypto:strong_rand_bytes(16)` FFI, insert with now), `Validate` (hit -> touch last_activity + return True; miss -> False), `Touch`, `AttachSse`/`DetachSse` (set/clear sse_subject), `Evict(now)`. Eviction self-schedules every 60s via `process.send_after`, dropping any session idle > 30 min (`idle_timeout_ms`). The actor Subject is published in persistent_term (`sessions_register`/`sessions_lookup` FFI) so the HTTP listener subtree, which boots after sessions, can `sessions.global()` it.

WIRING. `supervisor.gleam` picks transports from `config.transport` (Stdio | Http | Both | Disabled). For Http|Both it adds `sessions.start_supervised` then the mist listener (which reads `pool.global()` + `sessions.global()`); boot order ensures both globals exist first. For Stdio|Both it adds `stdio_worker.start_supervised` as a TRANSIENT child last (so pool.global() is populated; stdin EOF -> actor.stop() = clean exit, no restart). The pool lives in its own RestForOne subtree above both transports.

key_files.role: The server CORE and the transport-to-core boundary. `handle_line/2` is the single entry point both transports call; `DispatchResult` (Reply/NoReply/ProtocolError) is the contract; pure string-in/string-out dispatch by JSON-RPC method.

Stdio read loop as a supervised actor: owns the {fd,0,0} stdin port, selects raw port mailbox tuples, spawns one unlinked dispatcher per line (async), funnels all stdout writes back through itself, drains in-flight workers on EOF.
Thin NDJSON framing veneer over FFI: documents the no-Content-Length / unbuffered-stdout contract; `write/1` and `read_line/0` are @external to pharos_stdin_ffi.

The actual framing + unbuffered-IO mechanism: line-mode {fd,0,0} stdin port, decode_port_event, and write_line/1 (raw {fd,1,1} open->port_command->port_close per line to bypass the :user group-leader buffering under -noshell).

mist-based HTTP transport: router (POST /mcp, POST /mcp/respond, GET /mcp/events, GET /mcp), origin validation, body read+cap, session issue/validate, dispatch to handle_line, SSE stream + heartbeat, port-file discovery.
HTTP session table actor: Dict(SessionId, SessionState{last_activity_us, sse_subject}); Issue/Validate/Touch/AttachSse/DetachSse/Evict; idle eviction; persistent_term global for cross-subtree lookup.
ETS-backed in-flight dispatcher registry (stdio only) keyed by MCP id, enabling kill-based cancellation; defines the WriterMsg contract dispatchers use to send replies back to stdio_worker.

Transport wiring: chooses stdio_worker (transient) and/or sessions+http listener children based on config.transport; enforces boot order so pool.global()/sessions.global() are populated before consumers start.
Session id generator: 16 random bytes -> 32-char lowercase hex, header/URL-safe.

code_snippets.why_notable: THE transport-to-core boundary. One pure function, string in / tagged-union out, takes the shared Pool. Every transport calls exactly this; nothing transport-specific leaks in. This is the shape geex should copy.
HTTP side of the boundary: maps the exact same DispatchResult onto HTTP status codes. Compare to stdio_worker's dispatch_line which maps it onto stdout writes — same core, two adapters.

Stdio side of the boundary + the async-dispatch design: each line runs on its own process so the read loop never blocks, enabling mid-flight cancel; replies route back through the single writer Subject for line-atomic stdout.

code_snippets.snippet:
write_line(Body) when is_binary(Body) ->
    Port = erlang:open_port({fd, 1, 1}, [out, binary]),
    true = erlang:port_command(Port, [Body, $\n]),
    erlang:port_close(Port),
    nil.
code_snippets.why_notable: The keep-stdout-clean-and-unbuffered mechanism. Bypasses Erlang's buffering :user group leader entirely; close-per-write forces a synchronous flush so MCP hosts see the reply before their connect timeout. A naive println would hang initialize under a release runtime.

code_snippets.snippet:
stdin_port() ->
    case persistent_term:get(pharos_stdin_port, undefined) of
        undefined ->
            P = erlang:open_port({fd, 0, 0}, [in, binary, eof, {line, 65535}]),
            persistent_term:put(pharos_stdin_port, P),
            P;
        P -> P
    end.
code_snippets.why_notable: NDJSON read framing: a raw line-mode port over fd 0 delivers one `{eol, Line}` per `\n` directly to the owning actor's mailbox — no Content-Length parsing, and bypasses :user for per-line (not EOF-batched) delivery.

Everything tracked per HTTP session: just an idle timestamp (for eviction) and an optional SSE delivery channel. Minimal — session identity is decoupled from any protocol/LSP state, which lives in the shared Pool.

Session lifecycle: id minted on the `initialize` handshake and returned in the Mcp-Session-Id header; required and validated on every subsequent request. Matches the MCP Streamable HTTP spec's session model.

design_patterns: Thin-transport / pure-core seam: `handle_line(pool, String) -> DispatchResult` is the ONE boundary; each transport is a ~5-line adapter mapping the tagged result onto its wire (HTTP status codes vs stdout line). Transports never reach into dispatch internals.
Tagged-union return as the protocol-neutral reply: Reply | NoReply | ProtocolError lets each transport decide framing (200/204 vs write/no-write) without the core knowing the transport.
Single-writer actor for output serialization: all stdout writes funnel through the stdio_worker actor so concurrent dispatchers can't interleave half-lines (line-atomicity).
Async per-request dispatch via unlinked processes + ETS pid registry, enabling cooperative-and-forceful cancellation (send_exit) decoupled from LSP cooperation.

Selector merging of heterogeneous mailbox sources: one actor receives its own Msg, mapped WriterMsg from dispatchers (select_map), and raw OS-port tuples (select_other), unifying them into one typed Msg stream.
persistent_term as a typed service-locator: pool.global()/sessions.global() let later-booting subtrees find earlier actors' Subjects without threading them through child specs.
FFI escape hatch for runtime-environment quirks: raw fd ports to defeat the BEAM release runtime's stdio buffering, kept behind a Gleam-typed veneer (StdinResult, PortEvent).
Config-driven supervision topology: the same tree adds/omits stdio_worker vs sessions+listener children based on config.transport (Stdio/Http/Both/Disabled).
findings.type_safety_notes: Gleam models the boundary with a closed sum type `DispatchResult { Reply(String) | NoReply | ProtocolError(String) }`, so the compiler forces every transport's mapping to be exhaustive — both http.dispatch and stdio dispatch_line `case` over all three variants, and adding a fourth (e.g. a future `ServerRequest`) would fail to compile until each transport handles it. JSON-RPC ids are `Id { IntId(Int) | StringId(String) }`, preserving the spec's string-or-int id without stringly collapsing. The inbound message is split at decode time into `RequestMessage(id,...)` vs `NotificationMessage(...)` purely by presence of `id`, so 'notifications never get a reply' is enforced structurally, not by convention. The stdin port's raw mailbox tuples are narrowed through FFI into `PortEvent { PortLine | PortEof | PortOther }` and stdin reads into `StdinResult { StdinLine | StdinEof | StdinError }`, keeping untyped Erlang `Dynamic` at the very edge. Session SSE messages are a typed `SseMsg { Push | Heartbeat | Close }`. AN ELIXIR PORT LOSES ALL OF THIS at compile time: DispatchResult becomes a tagged tuple/atom like `{:reply, json} | :no_reply | {:protocol_error, json}` that each transport must pattern-match by discipline (a missed clause is a runtime FunctionClauseError, not a compile error); Id becomes a bare term needing runtime guards; the request/notification split and the port-event narrowing become defensive `case`/`with` clauses. The shared-Pool handle and the persistent_term globals translate cleanly (they're already Erlang runtime mechanisms), as do the OTP actors (GenServer), the unlinked dispatcher processes (Task/spawn), the ETS worker registry, and the raw-fd Port FFI (verbatim Erlang). So an Elixir port keeps the architecture 1:1 but must re-establish exhaustiveness via tests/Dialyzer typespecs rather than the compiler.
gotchas: stdout is sacred: it carries ONLY JSON-RPC frames. Any stray write (a debug println, a library that logs to stdout) corrupts the protocol stream. All logging goes to stderr/ring/file. This is enforced by never calling gleam/io.* on the stdout path — only pharos_stdin_ffi:write_line.

Under Burrito's `-noshell -mode embedded` release runtime, the default `:user` group leader BUFFERS stdout and only flushes on stdin EOF — but MCP hosts hold stdin open waiting for the reply, so initialize would hang past the host's 30s timeout. The fix is the raw {fd,1,1} port with close-per-write; a *cached* persistent stdout port was tried and left bytes queued indefinitely. Do not 'optimize' the per-write port-open away.
Stdin must likewise use a raw {fd,0,0} line-mode port, not :user, or reads only arrive at EOF (same buffering bug, read side).

Cancellation is asymmetric across transports: stdio registers each request in the request_workers ETS table and can kill the worker via send_exit; HTTP runs handle_line inline on the mist connection process and is NOT in that table, so notifications/cancelled is a deliberate no-op for HTTP (the handler logs the miss as normal).
When a worker is killed mid-flight by cancel, its own `request_workers.delete` cleanup never runs — the cancel handler in server.gleam must delete the entry itself or the ETS table leaks.

HTTP POST /mcp/respond and the SSE Push path are stubs/half-wired: /mcp/respond accepts and returns 204 without correlating to an in-flight server request; the SSE channel exists but nothing pushes server-initiated requests yet (Tier 2 / M8 stage 0).

Session id is required from the SECOND request onward; the first `initialize` mints it. is_initialize does a SEPARATE fast partial parse of just `method` before the core re-parses the whole body — two parses by design, to gate session issuance cheaply.
Body is capped at 4 MiB (max_body_bytes); larger requests are refused, not streamed.

stdin lines >65535 bytes arrive as noeol chunks; the port path concatenates overflow but the comment notes MCP lines are far below this, so the partial-line handling is essentially untested in practice.

Origin validation defaults to allowing NO-Origin requests (curl/native clients) plus localhost/127.0.0.1/[::1]; a reverse proxy that strips/rewrites Origin or a non-loopback bind needs this policy revisited or it will 403 legitimate clients.

geex_relevance.rationale: If geex is an Elixir MCP server (the StructuredOutput schema's type_safety framing implies an Elixir port target), this is a clean, production-tested reference architecture for serving one MCP core over both stdio and Streamable HTTP. The central insight — collapse the transport-to-core seam to a single pure `handle_line(state, raw_line) -> {reply|no_reply|protocol_error}` and make each transport a tiny adapter — ports directly and is the highest-value idea to copy. The stdio framing/flushing details are BEAM-runtime-specific and transfer almost verbatim to Elixir (same OTP/Port primitives), so they're concrete reusable knowledge, not just inspiration. The HTTP/SSE/session pieces are a sound skeleton but partly stubbed here, so geex should take the shapes (one /mcp POST endpoint, Mcp-Session-Id issued on initialize, a sessions GenServer keyed by id holding last_activity + optional SSE pid, idle eviction) and finish the bidirectional path itself.
geex_relevance.what_to_take: 1) The seam: define a single core entrypoint `handle_line(state, raw) :: {:reply, json} | :no_reply | {:protocol_error, json}` (or an MCP.Message struct) and keep every transport a thin mapper — this is the load-bearing design and ports 1:1 to Elixir. 2) The stdio runtime knowledge verbatim: open raw Ports on fd 0 (line mode, `{:line, 65535}`, `:binary`, `:eof`) and fd 1 (write Body++\n, then close to force a synchronous flush) to dodge the release-runtime `:user` group-leader buffering that otherwise hangs initialize; reserve stdout exclusively for frames and send all logs to stderr. 3) Async per-line dispatch on its own process + an ETS/Registry of in-flight request pids keyed by JSON-RPC id, so cancellations can kill the worker and the read loop never blocks; funnel all stdout writes through one GenServer for line-atomicity. 4) HTTP shapes: single POST /mcp, mint Mcp-Session-Id on the `initialize` request and require+validate it thereafter (400 on missing/unknown), 200 for Reply/ProtocolError and 204 for NoReply, 4 MiB body cap, loopback-only Origin allowlist for DNS-rebind defense, and an after_start port-file for OS-assigned-port discovery. 5) Sessions GenServer state shape: %{session_id => %{last_activity, sse_pid}} with periodic idle eviction. Skip/finish-yourself: the /mcp/respond correlation and SSE server-request push are stubs here.

findings.subsystem: MCP tool definition, tools/list generation, and tools/call dispatch/decoding (pharos-mcp)
findings.purpose: In pharos-mcp there is NO first-class "tool record" type. A "tool" is split across three hand-written, manually-kept-in-sync artifacts: (1) a thin per-tool implementation module (e.g. tools/hover.gleam) that exposes a single typed `handle(...)` function taking positional Gleam arguments and returning `Result(String, SomeError)`; (2) a per-tool `*_tool_definition() -> json.Json` builder function living in mcp/server.gleam that hand-writes the `{name, description, inputSchema}` JSON object including the full JSON Schema the LLM sees; and (3) a per-tool `decode_*_arguments(Option(Dynamic)) -> Result(tuple, String)` decoder plus a `handle_*` wrapper in server.gleam that decodes JSON arguments into the typed positional values, calls `.handle(...)`, and renders the result. These three are wired together by string-keyed name in two registries: `allowed_tool_definitions()` (name -> definition-builder, for tools/list) and the `dispatch_tool_call` case expression (name -> handler, for tools/call). Categories/filtering live in tools/registry.gleam keyed by the same string name a third time. This triple/quadruple hand-duplication keyed on a bare string is exactly the boilerplate geex's macro DSL wants to collapse into one declaration.
findings.how_it_works:
Lifecycle of one tool call:

1. tools/list — `dispatch` (server.gleam:113) routes JSON-RPC method "tools/list" to `tools_list_response(id)` (line 318), which wraps `allowed_tool_definitions()` under `{"tools": [...]}`. `allowed_tool_definitions()` (line 330) holds a hardcoded `curated` list of `#(name_string, builder_fn)` pairs (builder = `fn() -> Json`), appends `debug.named_definitions()` (same shape), then `list.filter_map`s: for each pair it calls `tool_registry.is_allowed(name)` and, if allowed, invokes `builder()` to instantiate the JSON. So the list is filtered by the cached config tool filter BEFORE the LLM ever sees it.

2. Each tool definition is a hand-written function returning `json.object([#("name", ...), #("description", ...), #("inputSchema", ...)])`. The inputSchema is itself a hand-written JSON Schema `json.object` with `"type": "object"`, a `"properties"` object, and a `"required"` array. There is NO derivation from the `handle` function's Gleam type signature — the schema is authored by hand and must be manually kept consistent with both the decoder and the handler's parameter list. Shared schema fragments are factored into helpers: `position_arg_schema()` (line 421, the uri/line/character/timeout_ms shape reused by hover, goto_definition, etc.) and `timeout_ms_property()` (line 399, the shared optional timeout arg). Tools either reuse `position_arg_schema()` wholesale (hover at line 487 just does `#("inputSchema", position_arg_schema())`) or inline a bespoke object (find_references at line 519 inlines because it adds `include_declaration`).

3. tools/call — routed to `handle_tool_call` (line 795). First `peek_filtered_name` decodes just the name and re-checks `tool_registry.is_allowed`; a denied tool returns JSON-RPC error -32601 "Tool not enabled". Otherwise `dispatch_tool_call` (line 824) calls `decode_tool_call(params)` (line 3067) which decodes the JSON-RPC params into `#(name: String, arguments: Option(Dynamic))` using a gleam/dynamic/decode decoder (`decode.field("name", decode.string)` + `decode.optional_field("arguments", ...)`). The result feeds a giant case expression matching `Ok(#("hover", arguments))`, `Ok(#("find_references", arguments))`, etc. — one arm per tool, each delegating to a `handle_*` function. A final catch-all `Ok(#(name, arguments))` arm delegates to `debug.dispatch(pool, name, arguments)` (its own internal string-keyed case), and `None` from that yields -32602 "Unknown tool". Bad params yield -32602 "Invalid tools/call params".

4. Argument decoding — each `handle_*` calls a `decode_*_arguments` helper that turns `Option(Dynamic)` into a typed tuple. Pattern (decode_find_references_arguments, line 2581): unwrap the Option (`option.to_result(args, "arguments object missing")`), build a gleam/dynamic/decode decoder with `use uri <- decode.field("uri", decode.string)`, `use line <- decode.field("line", decode.int)`, `decode.optional_field("include_declaration", True, decode.bool)` (note: the literal Gleam-side default `True` lives here, NOT in the schema — the schema only documents it in prose), `decode.optional_field("timeout_ms", None, decode.map(decode.int, Some))`, then `decode.success(#(...))`. On `decode.run` success it post-processes the timeout via `finalize_timeout(name, compiled_default, uri, user_arg)` which resolves the effective timeout through the session-override / pharos.toml / compiled-const stack (`resolve_tool_timeout`, line 1053). On decode failure it returns a hand-written human-readable `Error(string)` describing the expected shape (the decoder's structured error is discarded via `result.map_error`).

5. Handler delegation + result/error rendering — `handle_find_references` (line 1158) pattern-matches the decoded tuple, calls `find_references.handle(pool, uri, line, character, include_decl, timeout_ms)` (the thin impl module, which returns `Result(String, FindReferencesError)` where the Ok String is already JSON-encoded LSP output via `tool_helpers.json_encode`). It then renders: `Ok(json_text)` -> `success_response(id, fn() { tool_text_result(json_text, False) })`; each error variant -> `success_response(id, fn() { tool_text_result(reason, True) })`. Crucially, tool-level errors (LSP failures) are returned as MCP *successful* JSON-RPC responses with `isError: true` in the result body (NOT as JSON-RPC protocol errors) — only malformed params produce a real JSON-RPC -32602 error. `tool_text_result(message, is_error)` (line 3094) builds `{"content": [textBlock], "isError": bool}` (and logs to stderr when is_error). `success_response` wraps `{jsonrpc, id, result}`, `error_response` wraps `{jsonrpc, id, error: {code, message}}`.

Two registration styles coexist: the curated tier-1/tier-2 tools are spelled out individually in both `allowed_tool_definitions` and the `dispatch_tool_call` case; the debug/runtime tier uses a more data-driven `debug.named_definitions() -> List(#(String, fn() -> Json))` + `debug.dispatch(pool, name, args) -> Option(ToolResult)` pair — but it's still two parallel string-keyed lists/cases in one module. Both styles still hand-write the inputSchema JSON.

key_files.role: The heart of the subsystem. Holds tools_list_response, allowed_tool_definitions (name->builder registry), every *_tool_definition() JSON-Schema builder, position_arg_schema/timeout_ms_property shared schema helpers, handle_tool_call/dispatch_tool_call (name->handler registry), decode_tool_call, every decode_*_arguments + handle_* wrapper, and the response renderers (tool_text_result/success_response/error_response).

Representative thin impl module. Exposes `pub const default_timeout_ms`, a `HoverError` variant type, and `pub fn handle(pool, file_uri, line, character, timeout_ms) -> Result(String, HoverError)` that builds LSP params, runs the request through session, and json_encodes the result. No name/description/schema here at all.
Richer thin impl module: same shape as hover but `handle` adds an `include_declaration: Bool` positional arg and builds a nested `context.includeDeclaration` LSP param.

Cross-tool helpers: next_id (i32-bounded request ids), json_encode (Dynamic->JSON string FFI), describe_request_error (maps RequestError variants to LLM-facing strings), with_capability_gate (short-circuit if LSP didn't advertise the method).

Third string-keyed table: category_for(name)->ToolCategory (a giant string case) and is_allowed(name) combining the cached config filter with the category. Drives both the tools/list filter and the tools/call gate.

The data-driven registration variant: named_definitions() -> List(#(String, fn()->Json)) and dispatch(pool, name, args) -> Option(ToolResult). Worth studying as a lighter-weight pattern, though still hand-written schemas + parallel lists.
MCP content block type. `ContentBlock` is a one-variant type `Text(text)` with `to_json` producing {type:text, text:...}. This is the unit of tool output.

code_snippets.why_notable: The tools/list registry. THIS is the list a geex macro would generate. Note the tool is a `#(String, fn() -> Json)` pair, not a record — name is a bare string duplicated from the definition body and from the dispatch case and from registry.gleam.

code_snippets.why_notable: A full inputSchema written out by hand. This is the JSON-Schema-as-data shape geex must emit. Note the schema's `required` array and the boolean's default are described in prose only — the actual default lives separately in the decoder (True).

THE argument-decoding helper. Uses gleam/dynamic/decode's `use field <- decode.field(name, type)` applicative style to turn Option(Dynamic) into a typed tuple. The decoder field list, the schema properties, and the handle() parameter list are three parallel hand-maintained restatements of the same arg list — the core duplication geex should auto-generate from one source.
How tools/call params split into (name, raw-arguments-Dynamic). Arguments stay Dynamic until the per-tool decoder runs — a two-stage decode: outer envelope here, inner per-tool decoder in dispatch.

How handlers return results AND errors. Tool-level failures are MCP successes with isError:true (NOT JSON-RPC errors). Output is always a single text content block holding a JSON string. Only malformed params escalate to a real JSON-RPC -32602 via error_response.

The handler wrapper glue between dispatch and impl module: decode -> call impl handle() with positional typed args -> render. This boilerplate is identical in shape across ~25 tools and is the second thing geex's macro should generate (alongside the schema).

design_patterns: String-keyed parallel registries: the same tool name is restated as a bare string literal in at least 4 places — the definition builder body (name JSON), the allowed_tool_definitions pair key, the dispatch_tool_call case arm, and registry.gleam's category_for/is_allowed. No single source of truth; geex's macro is meant to collapse all of these.

Schema-as-data: JSON Schema is built with gleam/json combinators (json.object/json.array/json.string), not from any reflection of the Gleam handle() signature. inputSchema and the decoder are hand-synced.

Applicative JSON decoding via gleam/dynamic/decode: `use x <- decode.field("x", decode.T)` / `decode.optional_field(name, default, dec)` / `decode.success(tuple)` then `decode.run`. Defaults for optional args live in the decoder, not the schema.
Two-stage decode: outer envelope (name + raw Dynamic arguments) then per-tool inner decoder, keeping arguments as Dynamic across the dispatch boundary.

Errors as data, not exceptions: each impl module defines its own 2-variant error type (SessionFailed/RequestFailed), mapped to human strings by a per-module describe_* function; tool errors surface as MCP isError:true successes, only param errors become JSON-RPC errors.
Shared schema fragment helpers (position_arg_schema, timeout_ms_property) reduce but do not eliminate per-tool schema duplication.

Two coexisting registration styles: explicit per-tool functions (tier 1/2) vs. data-driven List(#(String, fn()->Json)) + dispatch returning Option (debug tier). The latter is closer to what a macro could target.
Config-driven filtering applied identically at list time (omit) and call time (refuse), both via tool_registry.is_allowed.
findings.type_safety_notes: Gleam models the handler as a fully-typed function (`handle(pool, uri: String, line: Int, character: Int, include_declaration: Bool, timeout_ms: Int) -> Result(String, FindReferencesError)`), and the error channel as a sum type per tool. But the type system does NOT connect that signature to the inputSchema JSON or to the decoder: all three are independently hand-written, so a mismatch (e.g. schema says `required: [uri]` but decoder uses decode.field for line) is a runtime/LLM-facing bug, not a compile error. The Dynamic boundary (Option(Dynamic) arguments) is where types are lost and re-established by decode.run; a decode failure collapses gleam/dynamic/decode's structured DecodeError into a discarded `_` and a hand-written prose string. The success payload is also stringly-typed: handlers return `Result(String, _)` where the String is already-serialized JSON (via json_encode of a Dynamic LSP response), so the MCP layer never sees a typed result structure — it just wraps the opaque JSON string in a text content block. An Elixir port would lose the per-tool error sum types (likely degrading to tagged tuples/`{:error, %SomeError{}}` or exceptions), lose compile-time guarantees on the handler arity/types entirely, and would lean even harder on a macro to keep schema + decoder + handler in sync since Elixir has no static check catching drift. The upside for an Elixir/macro port: because the three artifacts are already mechanically derivable from one arg list (name, type, required?, default, description), a macro that takes a single typed param spec can generate the JSON Schema property, the decoder field, and the handler argument binding together — which is precisely the duplication geex aims to remove and where a macro recovers most of the safety Gleam's compiler is NOT currently providing here.

geex_relevance.rationale: This is the single most important reference subsystem for geex: it is a complete, production MCP tool layer (tools/list generation, JSON-Schema-per-tool, tools/call routing, JSON->typed decoding, result/error rendering) — but it is implemented as deliberately hand-written, name-keyed, triply-duplicated boilerplate. That is exactly the pain a geex macro DSL exists to remove. geex should treat pharos's shapes as the *target output* of its macro, not as the authoring model to copy. The wire shapes (inputSchema JSON Schema, {content:[text], isError} result, JSON-RPC -32602 for bad params, config-filtered list) are correct and should be reproduced; the authoring ergonomics (parallel string-keyed registries, hand-synced schema/decoder/handler) are the anti-pattern to replace.
geex_relevance.what_to_take: Reproduce these concrete shapes as macro output: (1) The tool's MCP identity is exactly {name, description, inputSchema}; inputSchema is a JSON Schema object with type:object, properties (each {type, optional description}), and a required array. (2) A tool definition = name + description + an ordered arg list where each arg carries {field_name, json_type, required-or-default, description, gleam/elixir_type}. From that ONE arg-list a macro should emit all three pharos artifacts at once: the inputSchema property, the decoder field (decode.field vs decode.optional_field(default)), and the handler parameter binding — eliminating pharos's drift risk. (3) Mirror the two-stage decode: outer {name, arguments:Dynamic} envelope, inner per-tool decoder. (4) Mirror the result contract: handler returns Result(payload, error); Ok -> {content:[text(payload)], isError:false}; tool error -> same with isError:true (an MCP success, not a JSON-RPC error); only param/decode failure -> JSON-RPC error -32602. (5) Generate the registry from the same declarations so name appears exactly once (vs pharos's 4 copies), and fold the category/filter (registry.gleam is_allowed) into that single declaration too. (6) Consider the shared-fragment idea (position_arg_schema, timeout_ms_property) as composable arg-group mixins in the DSL. Study debug.gleam's List(#(String, fn()->Json)) + dispatch->Option(ToolResult) as the lighter data-driven pattern that's closest to a macro target. Do NOT port the per-tool decode_*_arguments / handle_* / *_tool_definition trio literally — that triplet is the boilerplate to auto-generate.

gotchas: There is no `Tool` record/type anywhere — searching for one will fail. A tool is an emergent concept spread across 3 modules and ~4 string-keyed tables. geex inventing a real Tool struct/record is a net improvement, not a deviation.

Tool name is a bare string literal duplicated in: the *_tool_definition body, the allowed_tool_definitions pair, the dispatch_tool_call case arm, and registry.gleam category_for. Drift between these silently breaks list/call/filter consistency at runtime with no compile error.

Optional-arg DEFAULTS live in the decoder (e.g. include_declaration default True at line 2589), NOT in the inputSchema — the schema only mentions the default in prose. A naive port that reads defaults from the schema would miss them.
Tool-level failures are returned as JSON-RPC *successes* with isError:true in the result body; only malformed params produce a real JSON-RPC error (-32602). Conflating these is a common MCP bug.

The filter is enforced twice: tools/list omits disallowed tools (filter_map) AND tools/call refuses them (peek_filtered_name -> -32601). Both must use the same is_allowed source or a hidden tool stays callable.

Result payloads are pre-serialized JSON strings (json_encode of a Dynamic LSP response), wrapped verbatim in a text block — the MCP layer never structures the result. The 'String' in Result(String, _) is opaque JSON, not human text.

Request ids are bounded to i32 (tool_helpers.next_id, modulo 2^31-1) specifically because rust-analyzer's lsp-server parses RequestId::Int as i32 — an LSP-transport quirk, not an MCP concern, but lives in the shared tool helpers.

decode failures discard gleam/dynamic/decode's structured DecodeError (result.map_error to a hardcoded prose string), so the LLM-facing 'expected ...' messages are hand-maintained per decoder and can drift from the actual decoder fields.

findings.subsystem: MCP JSON-RPC boundary: typed decode/encode in Gleam (pharos-mcp/src/pharos/mcp/server.gleam + tool helpers)
findings.purpose: pharos-mcp is an MCP server (LLM <-> LSP bridge) whose entire JSON-RPC 2.0 boundary is hand-written in Gleam against the gleam_json + gleam/dynamic/decode standard libraries. Inbound NDJSON lines are parsed into a typed Message sum (RequestMessage | NotificationMessage) via a composable Decoder; the dispatch is one big exhaustive case on method/tool-name; per-tool argument decoders turn the opaque params Dynamic into typed Gleam tuples/records, returning Result(_, String) so a decode failure becomes a JSON-RPC -32602 "Invalid params" error rather than a crash; outbound responses are built with json.object([...]) constructors and serialized with json.to_string. Notably, the declared dependency "pollux" (a Gleam JSON-RPC library, ADR-002) is NOT actually imported anywhere in src/ — the server reimplements pollux's envelope/Id/Response shapes by hand.
findings.how_it_works:
Lifecycle of one inbound message (all in /home/oof/pharos-mcp/src/pharos/mcp/server.gleam):

1. ENTRY + PARSE. `handle_line(pool, line)` calls `json.parse(line, message_decoder())`. gleam_json's `json.parse` does two things in one shot: lex/parse the JSON string AND run a `decode.Decoder` over the resulting Dynamic, returning `Result(Message, json.DecodeError)`. A parse/decode failure maps to `ProtocolError(error_response(None, -32700, "Parse error"))`. Success goes to `dispatch`.

2. CLASSIFY (decoder-driven sum-type construction). `message_decoder() -> decode.Decoder(Message)` is the canonical gleam/dynamic/decode "use"-callback pipeline:
   use method <- decode.field("method", decode.string)
   use maybe_id <- decode.optional_field("id", None, decode.optional(id_decoder()))
   use maybe_params <- decode.optional_field("params", None, decode.optional(decode.dynamic))
   case maybe_id { Some(id) -> decode.success(RequestMessage(id, method, maybe_params)) ; None -> decode.success(NotificationMessage(method, maybe_params)) }
   The presence/absence of "id" decides Request vs Notification AT DECODE TIME, producing different constructors of the `Message` sum. `params` is kept as opaque `decode.dynamic` (Option(Dynamic)) — deferred, decoded later per-method. `id_decoder()` uses `decode.one_of(decode.int |> decode.map(IntId), [decode.string |> decode.map(StringId)])` to model the JSON-RPC string|int id as a typed `Id` sum (IntId(Int) | StringId(String)).

3. DISPATCH. `dispatch` pattern-matches the `Message` sum exhaustively. RequestMessage routes on method string: "initialize" | "tools/list" | "tools/call" | other (-> -32601). NotificationMessage matches "initialized", "notifications/cancelled", and a catch-all — notifications return `NoReply` (no response written). The compiler enforces both arms of `Message` and (with the catch-alls) total coverage.

4. PER-TOOL ARG DECODE. `tools/call` -> `handle_tool_call` -> `decode_tool_call(params)` extracts `#(name, Option(Dynamic) arguments)`. `dispatch_tool_call` is a giant case on the `name` string (Ok(#("hover", args)) -> handle_hover(...), etc.). Each handler runs a method-specific argument decoder, e.g. `decode_position_with_timeout` builds an inline decoder:
   use uri <- decode.field("uri", decode.string)
   use line <- decode.field("line", decode.int)
   use character <- decode.field("character", decode.int)
   use timeout_arg <- decode.optional_field("timeout_ms", None, decode.map(decode.int, Some))
   decode.success(#(uri, line, character, timeout_arg))
   then `decode.run(raw, decoder)`. On Error it returns `Error("expected uri: string, line: int, ...")` which the caller turns into a -32602 error_response; on Ok it returns a typed tuple. Decoders return Result(typed_tuple, String) — the String is a human-readable schema hint shown to the LLM. There are ~20 of these argument decoders, one per tool shape (position, uri-only, item-with-timeout, rename, code_actions range, memory_save, etc.).

5. OUTBOUND ENCODE. Responses are built structurally, never string-concatenated. `success_response(id, build_result)` -> json.object([#("jsonrpc", json.string("2.0")), #("id", id_to_json(id)), #("result", build_result())]) |> json.to_string. `error_response(id, code, message)` builds the JSON-RPC error object likewise. `tool_text_result(message, is_error)` wraps a string in the MCP content-block shape {content:[{type:"text",text:...}], isError:bool} via the `content_block` module (a `ContentBlock` sum with a `to_json`). Tool *definitions* for tools/list (the JSON Schemas the host sees) are ALSO hand-built as nested `json.object`/`json.array`/`json.string` literals — ~3000 of the file's 4176 lines are these literal schema builders.

6. RE-ENCODING OPAQUE LSP PAYLOADS. LSP responses come back as Dynamic; rather than fully decode them, tool_helpers.gleam exposes `json_encode(value: Dynamic) -> String` via @external FFI to an Erlang module ("pharos_fs_ffi", "encode_json") wrapping OTP 27's json:encode/1. So opaque sub-payloads (hover contents, locations) are passed through to the LLM as a JSON string inside a text block WITHOUT being parsed into typed records — a deliberate "pass-through the parts we don't need to reason about" escape hatch.

design_patterns: Decoder-as-value / applicative decode pipeline: `use field <- decode.field(...)` callbacks compose small Decoders into a record/tuple decoder; gleam/dynamic/decode is the Gleam analog of Elixir Ecto changesets or a Zod schema, but checked structurally at the value boundary (Gleam has no runtime type reflection).

Sum type for protocol variants: Message = RequestMessage | NotificationMessage and Id = IntId | StringId make 'is this a request or notification' / 'string or int id' a compile-time-exhaustive match instead of a runtime nil/guard check.

Result(typed, String) at every decode site: a malformed inbound payload is a value (Error(reason)) that deterministically becomes a -32602 JSON-RPC error with an LLM-readable schema hint — never an exception, never a crash.

Deferred/opaque decoding: params kept as Option(Dynamic) until the method is known, then decoded by a method-specific decoder; LSP sub-payloads never decoded at all, just re-encoded via FFI. Decode only what you branch on.
Structural encoders: every outbound frame built with json.object/json.array/json.string and json.to_string — no string interpolation of JSON, so malformed output is impossible by construction.
Flat exhaustive dispatch as deliberate documentation ('the code reads as a menu the MCP host sees') rather than a registry/dynamic-dispatch table.
findings.type_safety_notes:
What the Gleam types buy at the MCP boundary: (1) Inbound classification is total — `Message`/`Id` sums force every consumer to handle Request vs Notification and int vs string id; the compiler rejects a missing arm. (2) Decode failure is a typed Result, not an exception — `decode.run` returns Error(decode_errors) which is funneled into a spec-compliant -32602/-32700, so a hostile or buggy client cannot crash the dispatcher with a wrong-typed field. (3) Outbound responses cannot be structurally malformed: json.object/json.to_string guarantees well-formed JSON, and pollux's Response(t)=Result(t,ErrorObject) (were it used) would even make result-XOR-error a compile-time invariant. (4) The decoder set is the single source of truth for accepted field types (uri:string, line:int, timeout_ms:int).

What an Elixir port LOSES / must enforce at runtime instead: Elixir has no compile-time sum types or exhaustiveness — RequestMessage/NotificationMessage become tagged tuples or %{} maps checked by guards/pattern matches the compiler does NOT verify for completeness (a forgotten notification method just falls through or raises). The decode pipeline must be replaced by hand-written pattern matches on a Jason-decoded map plus explicit is_binary/is_integer guards, or a schema library (Ecto embedded schemas / Norm / Drops / peri) to get equivalent validation — and that validation runs at runtime with no static guarantee that every field was checked. `Id` being string|int, `params` optional, `result` XOR `error` — all become runtime invariants you must remember to assert (exactly the optional-params bug ADR-002 flags in the Elixir `jsonrpc2_spec` package). The compiler will not tell you that a new tool handler forgot to decode an argument or returned the wrong response shape; you find out via tests or a client error. Net: Gleam moves "did I handle this protocol shape" from test/runtime to compile time; Elixir must re-acquire that confidence through schemas + guards + exhaustive tests.

findings.subsystem: MCP request concurrency, LSP worker pool, and supervision tree
findings.purpose: pharos-mcp is an MCP server (over stdio or HTTP) that fronts a fleet of real language servers (rust-analyzer, gopls, pyright, etc.). Concurrency is handled with an OTP-process-per-request model on top: every inbound JSON-RPC line spawns its own ephemeral dispatcher process, so the stdio reader never blocks on slow LSP work and cancellations can arrive and kill in-flight requests. A single long-lived "pool" actor owns a cache of warm LSP procs and, crucially, does its slow cold-start work off-actor in per-key spawn workers that report back by message. The whole thing is held up by a hand-built gleam_otp supervision tree (OneForOne root over RestForOne subtrees) plus an Erlang simple_one_for_one dynamic supervisor for the per-LSP child processes. Shared, concurrently-read state lives in ETS / persistent_term; mutable coordination state lives inside the pool actor.
findings.how_it_works:
Per-request concurrency (stdio path): stdio_worker is a single supervised actor that owns the stdin Port and is the sole writer to stdout. On each `{Port, {data, {eol, Line}}}` it calls `dispatch_line/2`, which does NOT process the line inline. Instead it peeks the JSON-RPC `id`, then `process.spawn_unlinked` a fresh dispatcher process. That dispatcher: (1) inserts `mcp_id -> self_pid` into the `pharos_request_workers` ETS table, (2) calls `server.handle_line(pool, body)` (the slow LSP dispatch), (3) sends the result back to stdio_worker via a `WriterMsg` Subject (`WriteResponse(json)` or `WorkerDone`), (4) deletes its ETS entry. So there is one OTP process per in-flight MCP request. stdio_worker tracks an `inflight` counter (incremented on dispatch, decremented on each Write/WorkerComplete) purely to drain cleanly on stdin EOF. Stdout writes funnel through stdio_worker's single mailbox, so concurrent dispatchers can finish in any order without interleaving partial lines. Cancellation: because the reader never blocks, a `notifications/cancelled` line is read promptly; its handler looks up the in-flight dispatcher pid via `request_workers.lookup/1` and `process.send_exit/2` kills it, short-circuiting even an uncooperative LSP. The ETS table (not actor state) backs this so the cancel handler can read it synchronously without a round-trip. On the HTTP transport each request runs on its own mist connection process directly and is NOT registered in this table (lookup returns Error there).

LSP worker pool: `pharos/lsp/pool` is a SINGLE actor (one `Subject(Msg)` registered in persistent_term, fetched by everyone via `pool.global/0`). It owns the cache `Dict(ProcKey, Proc)` keyed by `(language, workspace, server_id)`. The key insight (M14 refactor) is that the actor never does slow work itself. On `Get`: cache hit -> reply immediately; cache miss with an existing inflight entry -> append the caller's reply Subject to that key's waitlist (dedup: many concurrent gets for the same key share one spawn); cache miss with no inflight -> `spawn_worker` (an unlinked process) that runs the 30-90s LSP `initialize` handshake + `$/progress` drain + readiness probe loop off-actor, then posts `SpawnCompleted(key, result)` back into the pool's mailbox. The pool monitors each spawn worker (`spawner_monitors`) so a crash before completion fans `Error(SpawnerCrashed)` to all waiters instead of hanging them, and monitors each live LSP proc (`monitors`) so its DOWN evicts the cache entry ("structure-by-supervision, communication-by-monitoring"). The pool traps exits and routes stray EXIT/unknown messages to an `UnexpectedMessage` log branch so an unexpected link can't silently kill it. The actual LSP actors (`pharos@lsp@proc`) are NOT children of the pool — they are children of the Erlang `pharos_lsp_dyn_sup` (simple_one_for_one), spawned via FFI `start_child`, with their Subjects published into the `pharos_lsp_proc_subjects` ETS bridge that the pool reads back after start_child returns.

Supervision tree (supervisor.gleam, built with gleam_otp static_supervisor): pharos_root is OneForOne (intensity 5 / period 60). Children: a log_subtree (RestForOne: ring_keeper then log_writer, both permanent), a pool_subtree (RestForOne: pool actor permanent + dyn_sup as a structural supervisor child), then transport-conditional children — sessions actor + http_listener (permanent, HTTP/Both only, boot-ordered so sessions registers its global before the listener accepts), and stdio_worker (TRANSIENT, Stdio/Both only, added last so pool.global is populated). Transient stdio_worker means stdin EOF -> actor.stop() is treated as a clean program exit (no restart), while a crash restarts it. Every internal supervisor uses intensity 5 / period 60: 5 child failures in 60s tears the whole tree down so an external supervisor (systemd, Burrito wrapper, the MCP host) restarts pharos fresh rather than thrashing. The dyn_sup per-child restart is `transient` (crash restarts the LSP in place; operator-requested kill via terminate_child does not).

Boot wiring: this lives in `pharos.gleam:do_boot/0`, NOT in runtime.gleam (runtime.gleam is only typed FFI wrappers over BEAM BIFs for the introspection MCP tools). Order: `config.load()` into persistent_term first; then idempotent ETS-table inits that supervised children depend on (`diagnostics_cache.init`, `trace_ring.init`, `registry.init`, `inflight.init`, `request_workers.init`, `dyn_sup.init_subjects_bridge`, `capabilities.init`, `instance_track.init`); then `root_supervisor.start(config)`; then `register_root_supervisor` and finally `heartbeat.start()`. The heartbeat is deliberately NOT in the tree — it's a plain `process.spawn` tail-recursive loop linked to the main process that logs memory + BEAM process count every 60s; if its function panics they want it to surface, and on hard kill it's reaped with everything else. Its whole value is the idle timeline (a gap reveals roughly when pharos died silently).

Shared vs per-request state: shared/concurrently-read = the persistent_term pool Subject + several ETS tables (request_workers pid table, lsp_proc_subjects bridge, diagnostics cache, capabilities, registry, config). Mutable coordination state = inside the pool actor (cache, monitors, inflight waitlists, lsp_state state machine) and inside stdio_worker (inflight counter, draining flag), each owned by exactly one process. Per-request state = the ephemeral dispatcher process's stack during `handle_line`. Per-LSP state = each lsp_proc actor.

pool.get uses an effectively-infinite 86_400_000ms call_timeout on purpose: gleam_otp actor.call KILLS the caller on timeout (raises, no Result(_, Timeout)). The spawner self-bounds and always replies, so the caller is never timeout-killed.
stdio_worker.make_writer is a workaround for gleam_erlang having no public cast_subject: it creates a fresh Subject and the selector's select_map projects WriterMsg onto the actor's Msg type.
Pool traps exits + has an UnexpectedMessage/select_other branch specifically so a stray EXIT signal doesn't silently kill it and erase the cache via a supervisor restart with no crash trace.

A pool restart wipes the entire cache and drops in-flight spawn workers — recover_or_spawn mitigates because the lsp_proc children may survive (different supervisor) and can be recovered from the ETS bridge.

Probe loop has dead-LSP fast-fail (lsp_proc_dead_reason sentinel + is_alive pre-check + safe_call_0 wrapper) because a dead lsp_proc Subject would otherwise panic the spawn worker via actor.call on a Noproc.
intensity 5/60 means 5 child crashes in 60s collapses the whole tree by design — not a bug; it hands recovery to the external supervisor.
findings.type_safety_notes: Gleam's typed actors model this well and most of it ports to Elixir only by convention. The pool's `Msg` is an opaque sum type, so the compiler guarantees `handle_message` is exhaustive over every message variant (Get/Evict/SpawnCompleted/ProcDown/...) and that each reply Subject carries the exact `Result(Proc, GetError)` shape. `Subject(Msg)` is a phantom-typed mailbox handle: a dispatcher physically cannot send the pool a message the pool didn't declare. `WriterMsg` (request_workers) is a separately-typed dispatch contract projected onto stdio_worker's `Msg` via select_map — the boundary between dispatcher and reader is type-checked end to end. `Pool` and `Worker` are opaque single-constructor wrappers, so the Subject can't be confused with any other Subject in the program. An Elixir port loses all of this: GenServer `handle_call`/`handle_cast` clauses match untyped tuples, exhaustiveness is runtime FunctionClauseError not compile error, reply shapes are unenforced, and there is no phantom typing keeping the request_workers WriterMsg distinct from the pool's Msg — you'd lean on tests, dialyzer specs, and discipline. The ETS bridge (proc subjects, request_workers pid table) is already effectively untyped at the BEAM level in both languages, so that part ports 1:1. The LspState/SpawnSpec records port to structs cleanly but their invariants (Spawning -> Probing -> Ready/Failed transitions in advance_state) become runtime-checked rather than type-guided.

findings.purpose: pharos is an MCP server that bridges LLMs to LSP servers. There are two boot entry points that converge on the same idempotent `boot/0`: (1) `pharos.main/0` for the `mix start` / dev path, and (2) `pharos_app_ffi:start/2` (the OTP application start callback) for the Burrito-wrapped release binary path. Both parse argv for meta flags (--version, --help, --doctor, --purge-cache, --cleanup, --print-default-config, --print-language-config) that short-circuit and exit, then resolve a single `Config` record from a layered precedence chain (compiled defaults < global TOML < project TOML < PHAROS_* env vars), park it in persistent_term, build a supervised tree whose children are chosen by `Config.transport` (Stdio | Http | Both | Disabled), and block forever. There are no runtime-configuration CLI flags — every knob is TOML or env. MCP hosts launch it simply as `command: "pharos"` (stdio transport by default), spawned as a subprocess speaking JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout.
findings.how_it_works:
ENTRY POINTS. Two paths, both idempotent via `pharos:boot/0`:

1. `pharos.main() -> Nil` (src/pharos.gleam:53). Used by `mix start` (mix.exs alias `start: ["run -e \":pharos.main()\""]`) and dev shells. Sequence: `redirect_erl_crash_dump()` (FFI, points ERL_CRASH_DUMP at ~/.cache/pharos/log so a BEAM panic does not pollute the invoker's cwd) → `handle_meta_flags(argv())`. If a meta flag fired it returns `Handled` and main exits doing nothing; otherwise `Continue` → `boot()`. On `Ok(pid)` it reads the cached config, logs `"pharos starting (transport=...)"`, runs `post_boot_dispatch()` (warm-and-exit subcommand vs. PHAROS_WARM_LANGS background warmup), then `process.sleep_forever()`.

2. `pharos_app_ffi:start(_Type, Args)` (src/pharos_app_ffi.erl:26). The Burrito release boots the BEAM and starts the `:pharos` OTP application; application_controller calls this. `main/0` is NOT called in release mode, so this callback re-runs the meta-flag dispatch via `pharos:dispatch_meta_or_continue()` (pharos.gleam:105) — `true` → `halt(0)`, else falls through to `pharos:boot()` and returns the supervisor pid (making the supervisor the application's primary process), then runs `post_boot_dispatch()`. A test-only `auto_boot: false` proplist makes it spawn an idle child instead so gleeunit suites can stand up scoped trees. `stop/1` clears the instance tracking dir.

BOOT. `boot() -> Result(Pid, String)` (pharos.gleam:122) is idempotent: if `find_root_supervisor()` (FFI; looks up the registered name `pharos_root_supervisor`) finds a live pid it returns it, else `do_boot()`. `do_boot()` (pharos.gleam:129): FIRST `config.load()` parks the resolved Config in persistent_term (downstream readers — log, http, registry, runtime tools — consult the cached value, never env/files directly), THEN runs a series of idempotent pre-supervisor ETS/init calls (diagnostics_cache, trace_ring, registry.init [must run AFTER config.load so language overrides are merged], inflight, request_workers, dyn_sup bridge, capabilities, instance_track, log_rotate boot sweep, SASL capture handler). It then computes `resolved_transport`: if argv parses as a `pharos warm ...` subcommand it forces `root_supervisor.Disabled` (boots pool+ETS but NO transport, so stdin EOF cannot race the warm-then-exit init:stop), otherwise `map_transport(cfg.transport)`. It builds a `root_supervisor.Config` carrying transport + all log/http fields and calls `root_supervisor.start(...)`. On success it registers the supervisor pid and starts a linked heartbeat process.

TRANSPORT SELECTION. `map_transport` (pharos.gleam:223) maps `config.Stdio/Http/Both` → `root_supervisor.Stdio/Http/Both`. The actual wiring is in supervisor.gleam `start/1`. Root is OneForOne (intensity 5 / period 60). It always adds the log_subtree (RestForOne: ring_keeper + writer) and pool_subtree (RestForOne: pool actor + dyn_sup). Then two transport-gated case expressions add children:
  - HTTP children: `case config.transport { Stdio | Disabled -> root; Http | Both -> root |> add(sessions.start_supervised) |> add(http.start_supervised(pool, sessions, port, bind)) }`. Boot order matters: sessions must register its global before the listener accepts connections.
  - Stdio child: `case config.transport { Http | Disabled -> root_with_http; Stdio | Both -> root_with_http |> add(transient_worker(stdio_worker.start_supervised)) }`. stdio_worker is TRANSIENT: stdin EOF returns `actor.stop()` (clean exit, no restart) while a dispatch crash restarts it. It is last in boot order so pool.global() is populated when its initialiser runs.
So: Stdio = log + pool + stdio_worker; Http = log + pool + sessions + http listener; Both = all of them; Disabled (warm subcommand) = log + pool only, no transport. Stdio/Both terminate via stdin EOF; Http-only has no stdin termination signal and relies on SIGTERM (hence `process.sleep_forever()`).

STDIO RUNTIME (stdio_worker.gleam). A single supervised actor owns stdout. Each inbound JSON-RPC line read from the stdin port is handed to an unlinked dispatcher process (pharos/mcp/request_workers) that calls mcp/server.handle_line/2 and sends the reply back as a `Write` message; the worker writes it as one stdout line. This async hand-off lets the worker keep reading (so notifications/cancelled can arrive mid-flight). An `inflight` counter tracks outstanding dispatchers so EOF can drain before shutdown.

CLI PARSING. argv comes from `pharos_runtime_ffi:argv/0` (FFI, returns user args after BEAM/Erlang flags). `handle_meta_flags` (pharos.gleam:268) → `match_meta` (pharos.gleam:316). Two-arg `--print-language-config <id>` (also `=`-joined form) is matched first via `match_print_language_config`, then a `list.fold_until` recognises single flags: `--version`/`-V`, `--help`/`-h`, `--print-default-config`, `--doctor`, `--purge-cache`, `--cleanup` (dry-run unless `--yes` present → `Cleanup(True)`). Each Handled branch prints/acts and returns `Handled`. `--doctor`/`--purge-cache`/`--cleanup` delegate to pharos/cli.gleam which run BEFORE the supervised tree and share the same `config.load()` path but never spawn pool/HTTP. The `warm` subcommand is NOT a meta flag — it boots the tree (Disabled transport) and is handled in `post_boot_dispatch` / `parse_warm_args` (`pharos warm rust typescript` or `pharos warm --all`).

CONFIG (config.gleam). `Config` record fields: transport (Transport=Stdio|Http|Both), tools (ToolFilter list of category aliases or literal tool names; default `["default"]`), http (HttpConfig: port [3535], bind ["127.0.0.1"], port_file [None]), log (LogConfig: filter_spec, file, ring_enabled [True], stderr_enabled [True], file_max_bytes, file_keep_rotated [3]), lsp (LspConfig: trace [False]), runtime (RuntimeConfig: trace_calls_enabled [False]), bridge (BridgeConfig: port [None] — VSCode bridge), languages (Dict of per-language overrides, flat or per-server array shape), tool_config (Dict of per-tool / per-tool×per-lang default_timeout_ms). `load()` = `defaults() |> overlay_global_toml |> overlay_project_toml |> apply_env` then `store_persistent`. Global TOML path: `PHAROS_CONFIG_FILE`, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pharos/pharos.toml`, else `$HOME/.config/pharos/pharos.toml`. Project TOML: `.pharos.toml` walked up from cwd (stops at fs root). TOML applied as overlay (missing keys leave prior value). Env overrides (apply_env): PHAROS_TRANSPORT, PHAROS_TOOLS (CSV), PHAROS_HTTP_PORT/BIND/PORT_FILE, PHAROS_LOG/LOG_FILE/LOG_RING/LOG_STDERR, PHAROS_TRACE_LSP, PHAROS_RUNTIME_TRACE_ENABLED, PHAROS_BRIDGE_PORT. Notable: PHAROS_LOG_FILE unset AND no TOML file → auto per-PID per-timestamp path under ~/.cache/pharos/log/. Tool filter resolution (tool_allowed/3): `"all"` exposes everything, `"default"` resolves to read+write+memory categories plus a 5-tool CatDebug allowlist (echo + 4 runtime_* recovery tools). env.gleam is a one-function FFI wrapper: `env.get(name) -> Option(String)`, None when unset, Some("") when set-empty.

INVOCATION. MCP hosts launch the binary as a subprocess with no args. README config (claude_desktop / Cursor / ChatGPT): `{"mcpServers": {"pharos": {"command": "pharos"}}}` (Cursor args `[]`). Default transport is stdio, so the host speaks JSON-RPC over the process's stdin/stdout. To pre-warm on every spawn, set `PHAROS_WARM_LANGS` (CSV) in the host config env. The one-shot `pharos warm <lang>...` CLI form boots, warms, and exits.
