design_patterns: Dual convergent entry points (main/0 for dev + OTP application start/2 for release) both funnel into one idempotent boot/0 that uses a registered-name lookup to avoid double-spawning the tree
Config-as-persistent_term: resolve once at boot, park in persistent_term, every downstream consumer reads O(1) lock-free via cached/0 and never touches env/files itself
Layered overlay precedence (defaults < global TOML < project TOML < env) with TOML-as-overlay semantics (missing keys preserve prior value) implemented as a pipe of pure overlay functions

Transport as an explicit ADT (Stdio|Http|Both|Disabled) that selects supervised children via case expressions, with a synthetic Disabled mode for the warm-and-exit CLI subcommand so no transport races the init:stop
Meta-flags short-circuit before boot and return a 2-variant outcome (Handled|Continue); the same dispatcher is re-invoked from the release path because main/0 is skipped there
Transient stdio worker: EOF = clean stop (no restart), crash = restart — encoding program-lifecycle semantics directly in the OTP restart strategy
Async stdout-owning actor: a single actor serialises stdout writes while unlinked dispatcher processes do the LSP work concurrently, preserving line-atomicity and enabling mid-flight cancellation
gotchas: main/0 is NOT called in the Burrito release — the OTP application controller calls pharos_app_ffi:start/2 instead, which is why meta-flag dispatch had to be duplicated there via dispatch_meta_or_continue/0; forgetting this means --doctor/--purge-cache/--cleanup silently fall through to normal boot.
config.load() MUST run before registry.init() (and the rest of do_boot's ETS init) because registry.init merges Config.languages over bundled defaults by reading persistent_term.

The `warm` subcommand is NOT a meta flag — it boots the full tree with transport forced to Disabled, then warms and calls init:stop. post_boot_dispatch waits for the :pharos app to be registered as :running before init:stop, else a fast warm leaves application_controller half-started and the stop/1 instance-dir cleanup never fires (leaks).
Http-only mode has no stdin EOF termination signal, so main relies on process.sleep_forever() + SIGTERM; only Stdio/Both terminate via stdin EOF through the transient stdio_worker.

Two transport-config decoders coexist: top-level `transport = "..."` AND `[server] transport = "..."`; both call parse_transport, and an unrecognised value keeps the prior value (logged warn) rather than erroring.

PHAROS_LOG_FILE unset together with no TOML log.file does NOT mean stderr-only — it auto-defaults to a per-PID per-timestamp file under ~/.cache/pharos/log/ (changed to avoid multi-instance clobbering). Set PHAROS_LOG_FILE="" (empty) to truly disable the file sink.
env.get returns Some("") for a set-but-empty var (not None), and several call sites special-case the empty string (e.g. PHAROS_CONFIG_FILE, PHAROS_TOOLS, PHAROS_HTTP_BIND) — the distinction matters.

persistent_term writes are global mutable state; load/0 is documented idempotent (re-call replaces), but two concurrent boots in one VM would race — guarded in practice by the registered-name idempotency check in boot/0.

io.println routes through Erlang's :user group leader which is flaky under the release's -noinput stdio; --print-language-config deliberately bypasses it via the pharos_stdin_ffi:write_line FFI writing directly to fd 1.

findings.type_safety_notes: Gleam models the whole surface with exhaustive ADTs that an Elixir port would have to enforce by hand. `Transport` (Stdio|Http|Both at config level, plus Disabled at supervisor level) is matched exhaustively in map_transport and in the two supervisor case expressions — the compiler guarantees every transport has a defined child set; in Elixir these would be atoms (:stdio/:http/:both/:disabled) with no exhaustiveness check, so a new mode could silently fall through a `case` and start no transport. The meta-flag flow uses a 2-variant `MetaOutcome` (Handled|Continue) and a `MetaFlag` ADT (with `Cleanup(Bool)` carrying the apply flag and `PrintLanguageConfig(String)` carrying the language) — in Elixir these become tagged tuples ({:cleanup, true}) validated only at runtime. Config is a deeply nested record of records with `Option(T)` fields distinguishing unset (None) from set; an Elixir port would use a struct with `nil` for unset, losing the compiler's None/Some discipline and forcing nil-guards everywhere (the empty-string-vs-None distinction around env.get is already a runtime concern even in Gleam). The TOML decoders return `Result`/`Option` and fall back to the prior value on decode failure — Elixir would lean on `with`/pattern matches or a library like Ecto.Changeset to recover the same overlay-preserves-prior semantics. ToolFilter/ToolCategory + tool_allowed/3 encode the alias-vs-literal resolution as pure functions over a List(String) and an enum; a port keeps the logic but loses the category exhaustiveness guarantee (CatRead|CatWrite|CatDebug|CatRaw|CatMemory). The FFI boundary (argv, env.get, persistent_term store/load, crash-dump redirect) is already Erlang, so it ports to Elixir essentially unchanged.

geex_relevance.rationale: This is a clean, battle-tested reference design for an MCP-server entry point and config system in the BEAM ecosystem, directly analogous to what geex needs. The shapes (layered config precedence, persistent_term caching, transport-as-ADT selecting supervised children, meta-flag short-circuit before boot, transient stdio worker with EOF=clean-exit semantics, dual entry points converging on an idempotent boot) are all reusable concepts. But it is Gleam-on-BEAM with Gleam-specific supervisor/actor libraries and a Burrito/Mix release story; if geex is Elixir these port as patterns, not code, and if geex targets a different runtime they are reference-only for the architecture.
geex_relevance.what_to_take: 1) The config precedence chain: compiled defaults < global TOML (XDG/HOME) < project file walked up from cwd < ENV-prefix overrides, resolved once and cached in persistent_term, with every consumer reading the cache rather than re-reading env/files. 2) Transport as an explicit enum that selects which supervised children start (stdio worker vs HTTP listener+sessions vs both), plus a Disabled mode for one-shot CLI subcommands so no transport races shutdown. 3) Meta-flags (--version/--help/--doctor/--print-default-config) that short-circuit and exit before any tree boots, sharing the same config-resolution path as a real boot (doctor as both diagnostic AND cache-warmup is a nice touch). 4) The transient stdio-worker contract: stdin EOF => actor.stop (no restart, clean program exit), crash => restart; single actor owns stdout while unlinked dispatchers do work concurrently (enables mid-flight cancellation). 5) MCP-host launch convention: bare `command: "pharos"`, stdio by default, env-var (PHAROS_WARM_LANGS) for per-spawn warmup. 6) The dual-entry-point + idempotent-boot pattern (registered-name guard) so dev-run and packaged-release share one boot path — and the gotcha that the release path bypasses main/0 so meta-flag dispatch must be re-invoked from the app start callback.

findings.subsystem: Project architecture narrative + stated design rationale (README, CHANGELOG, doc/architecture.md, ADRs 001/002/003/006/010/012/013, .private roadmap & future-improvements)
findings.purpose: pharos-mcp is a "headless LSP-MCP bridge for AI agents" — a long-lived Gleam/BEAM process that an MCP client spawns over stdio, which spawns and pools real language servers (rust-analyzer, gopls, jdtls, pyright, gleam-lsp, 23 langs total) and re-shapes LSP results into a curated, hand-typed MCP tool surface (53 tools). The project's self-stated thesis is that a JSON-RPC bridge is "nothing but passing typed messages around," so a statically-typed BEAM language (Gleam) + a type-parametric JSON-RPC library (pollux) eliminate a whole class of protocol-shape bugs at compile time while keeping OTP's supervision/concurrency for managing N supervised LSP subprocesses. The docs are unusually rigorous: 30 numbered ADRs capture the "why," an operational architecture.md maps every process/timeout/sync-boundary, and private docs capture lessons-learned and a roadmap.
findings.how_it_works:
CONTROL FLOW (from README "How it works" + doc/architecture.md): MCP client spawns pharos as a child for the session lifetime. Agent calls an MCP tool over stdio (e.g. find_references(uri,line,char)). Pharos detects language from the file URI extension via a registry, looks up the configured LSP. On a (language, workspace) cache miss it spawns the LSP as a subprocess, runs initialize handshake + a readiness probe (ADR-024), forwards the request as the corresponding LSP method, shapes the LSP reply into the tool's MCP return schema, ships it back. The LSP stays cached/pooled for the pharos process lifetime; subsequent calls reuse it. Multi-language workspaces run multiple LSPs side-by-side; multi-server languages (python=pyright+ruff) use method routing (ADR-019). "No background daemon" — pharos lives only as long as the spawning client; on stdin EOF it drains in-flight requests, sends shutdown/exit to each LSP, removes its instance-tracking dir, and halts.

PROCESS/SUPERVISION MODEL (doc/architecture.md + ADR-013/017): a pharos_root supervisor (one_for_one, 5/60 restart intensity) over: log_subtree (rest_for_one: ring_keeper + log_writer), pool_subtree (rest_for_one: pool_actor + lsp_dyn_sup which is a simple_one_for_one Erlang shim because gleam_otp doesn't expose that strategy), sessions_actor + http_listener_subtree (only for HTTP/Both transport), and stdio_worker (transient — clean stdin EOF returns actor.stop and the supervisor lets it die without restart). Each LSP is one lsp_proc GenServer (transient restart) owning one OS Port to the language server; it hosts request-id correlation, server-request handler dispatch, $/progress tracking, and pending-reply Subjects. The pool independently process.monitors each lsp_proc and evicts its cache entry on DOWN — "structure-by-supervision, communication-by-monitoring" (ADR-013). Out-of-tree state lives in ETS/persistent_term tables (proc subjects, request workers, inflight, diagnostics cache, session overrides).

CONCURRENCY (post-M14 refactor, architecture.md "pool spawn lifecycle"): the pool actor's handler returns FAST — actual LSP spawn+handshake+readiness runs in a separate process.spawn_unlinked spawner per cache-miss key, so cold-starts of different LSPs run in parallel and same-key cold-starts dedupe to one spawner with N waiters via an inflight waitlist. The CALLER of pool.get still blocks on an actor.call until SpawnCompleted. Same-LSP tool calls serialize at the proc actor mailbox (matches LSP's single-stream Port); different-LSP calls run fully parallel. stdio_worker dispatches each JSON-RPC line to its own spawn_unlinked worker (M10 async refactor) and is a single stdout write funnel so concurrent dispatchers never interleave.

JSON-RPC TYPE SAFETY (ADR-001/002): three surfaces speak JSON-RPC 2.0 (MCP stdio, MCP HTTP, LSP stdio). pollux (Gleam hex pkg by crowdhailer) is used directly with no wrapper. Its type-parametric Request(r,n) makes Notification a variant (exhaustive pattern matching), Id is a StringId/NumberId sum, and Response uses Result(t, ErrorObject) so a response can't carry both result and error. pollux already handles MCP's optional params (the source literally comments "// In mcp there are optional fields"), fixing exactly the bug the Elixir alternative jsonrpc2_spec has (its Request.parse requires a params key). No JSON-RPC batch support (removed from MCP 2025-03-26, unused by LSP).

TIMEOUTS (architecture.md "Timeout map", ADR-021): a 15-row layered timeout model. Resolution stack at request time: per-call timeout_ms arg > session override (runtime_set_tool_timeout ETS) > [tool_config.<name>.<lang>] > [tool_config.<name>] > compile-time per-tool default (30s, 60s for find_references). Spawn-side timeouts (initialize_timeout_ms 90s/180s scala, readiness_timeout_ms 30s, pool.get outer call = initialize+30s, proc.request outer call = timeout+5s) layer rather than compete.

LIFECYCLE HARDENING (ADR-030, README troubleshooting): graceful drain on stdin EOF/SIGTERM (PHAROS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_MS), orphan-LSP tracking under ~/.local/share/pharos/instances/<pid>/ with a verify-process-name-before-kill cleanup CLR, a try/catch logger handler that drops events when fd2 is gone (fixes pre-main boot panics on closed stderr), and a gating crash-repro suite of six failure modes.

Off-actor spawn (post-M14 / ADR-025): the pool GenServer handler never blocks on the 30-90s LSP cold start; it returns fast and a spawn_unlinked spawner per cache-miss key does the work, with an inflight waitlist deduping same-key concurrent callers

ADR-driven decision record: 30 numbered ADRs with Context/Decision/Consequences(Easier/Harder/Living-with)/Alternatives, plus a pre-implementation 'pin the design before we litigate it mid-refactor' convention (ADR-012, ADR-013)
findings.type_safety_notes:
The project's entire raison d'etre for Gleam is compile-time protocol-shape safety, and ADR-001 says so explicitly: 'the protocol-heavy nature of the project (every layer is JSON-RPC envelopes flowing in and out) is a good fit — type errors at compile time eliminate a class of bugs the runtime-validation path (TS+zod or Elixir+jsonrpc2_spec) only catches at runtime.' Concretely Gleam models: (1) JSON-RPC envelopes via pollux Request(r,n) — Notification is a sum variant so pattern matching is exhaustiveness-checked, Id is StringId/NumberId, Response is Result(t, ErrorObject) so a malformed response is unrepresentable; (2) each curated tool as a typed Params record + typed result (ADR-006) so 'adding a new tool is a Gleam module that won't compile if shapes are wrong'; (3) OTP child specs that 'declare their message types' (ADR-001); (4) per-language readiness_token: Option(String) and workspace_configuration: Option(Json) so 'None means no wait' is encoded in the type, not a magic value; (5) the future-improvements ToolError(kind: ToolErrorKind, message) proposal would lift error classification from string-grepping into a sum type.

An ELIXIR PORT would lose almost all of this at compile time and have to re-enforce it at runtime: pollux's typed Request(r,n)/Response Result-XOR becomes either hand-rolled structs (the jsonrpc2_spec path, which ADR-002 documents as buggy on optional params and lacking a Notification type) or dynamic maps validated at the boundary; exhaustive pattern matching on JSON-RPC variants becomes runtime case clauses with no compiler guarantee a variant is handled; the 'won't compile if tool shapes are wrong' guarantee becomes a test-suite obligation. The OTP layer ports cleanly (gleam_otp IS Erlang OTP underneath; the simple_one_for_one piece is already an Erlang shim, src/pharos_lsp_dyn_sup.erl — so an Elixir DynamicSupervisor would actually be MORE idiomatic there). Net: an Elixir port keeps the concurrency/supervision model verbatim but trades the compile-time JSON-RPC/tool-shape guarantees for runtime validation (zod-equivalent discipline). The docs frame this exact tradeoff as the project's core bet.
gotchas: 'No background daemon' is a deliberate v0.1 stance, not a permanent one: pharos dies with its spawning MCP client and re-spawns/re-indexes LSPs per session. roadmap.md v0.2 item #3 ('pharos as a service' daemon + idle-timeout lifecycle + TLS) is the planned reversal — geex should decide its session/daemon model up front rather than inherit the per-spawn-cold-start cost

Cold start dominates everything: jdtls 5-15min on big repos, HLS 5+min, metals 2-3min. The M14 finding (architecture.md) is that even after the off-actor pool refactor, the CALLER of pool.get still blocks until SpawnCompleted, so a slow first call still times out a harness — parallelism only helps ACROSS languages. Warmup (pharos warm / PHAROS_WARM_LANGS) is the mitigation, and a 'warmup probe' (retry workspace/symbol until non-error) is a named future fix

HTTP transport is second-class: architecture.md notes the HTTP path does NOT populate pharos_request_workers, so cancel over HTTP only fires the LSP-side $/cancelRequest, not the worker-kill arm. SSE proxies idle-timeout at 60-120s; pharos's 15s heartbeat defeats most but not all (ADR-012)

workspace/applyEdit declines by default (ADR-012 decision 7) — a server that emits an applyEdit outside the rename/code-actions path silently fails to write. Correct safety default for an LLM bridge, surprising for direct LSP passthrough

tsserver pushes NO diagnostics until it receives workspace/didChangeConfiguration after initialized, and pulls workspace/configuration during init — without a handler it times out and degrades (ADR-010). Any LSP bridge must do sync (not async) config push before unblocking tool dispatch, or get flaky diagnostics

Per-LSP actor mailbox is a hard serialization point (ADR-013 'living with'): a 30s find_references queues all other calls to that same LSP behind it. pharos 'cannot work around an LSP's serialization with more concurrency'

No dep-directory edit guard yet (future-improvements 'Edit safety'): apply_workspace_edit/edit_at_symbol/format_document against node_modules/.venv/.cargo would actually persist and corrupt an installed dependency. Only virtual jdt:// URIs are guarded (ADR-029). geex should add path-based guards from day one
gleam_otp does not expose simple_one_for_one, forcing an Erlang FFI shim (src/pharos_lsp_dyn_sup.erl) — a concrete Gleam ecosystem gap to expect
Elixir 1.19.5 emits an unsuppressable 16-line Logger :backends deprecation warning at every BEAM boot regardless of config (future-improvements) — a known BEAM-stack papercut
Local benchmark cost numbers underestimate billed cost ~4.5x (README) — methodology caveat, not load-bearing for relative deltas

geex_relevance.rationale: pharos-mcp is the closest possible prior art to a Gleam/BEAM MCP-LSP server and its ADRs are an exceptionally well-reasoned, honestly-caveated design record — but the task scope is to capture what the project SAYS about its architecture and why-Gleam, and geex is (per the StructuredOutput schema's framing) evaluating an Elixir port. The value here is the rationale and the lessons, not the literal Gleam code, which doesn't port verbatim. The compile-time-JSON-RPC-safety thesis is the one thing geex must consciously decide whether to keep (port to a typed boundary in Elixir, e.g. a pollux-equivalent or strict zod-style runtime validation) or knowingly drop.
geex_relevance.what_to_take: 1) ADOPT the supervision/concurrency shape near-verbatim — it ports cleanly to Elixir (gleam_otp is OTP; the simple_one_for_one shim becomes an idiomatic DynamicSupervisor): root one_for_one 5/60 over pool_subtree (pool GenServer + DynamicSupervisor of one-proc-per-LSP), one GenServer per LSP owning one Port, pool monitors each worker and evicts cache on DOWN, transient stdio worker that stops cleanly on EOF. 2) ADOPT off-actor spawn (ADR-025): never block the pool GenServer on a 30-90s LSP cold start; spawn the handshake in a Task and dedupe same-key callers via an inflight waitlist. 3) ADOPT the curated-typed-tools + one raw escape hatch philosophy (ADR-006) over auto-gen — and the edit-as-data safety stance (only one tool mutates disk, dry_run default). 4) ADOPT the layered timeout resolution stack (ADR-021) and the sync-config-push-before-dispatch fix for tsserver (ADR-010). 5) DECIDE EARLY on the two things pharos deferred and now regrets the shape of: the daemon/session lifecycle (roadmap v0.2 #3) and dep-directory edit guards (future-improvements). 6) REPLICATE the documentation discipline: numbered ADRs with Easier/Harder/Living-with + a single operational architecture.md with a timeout map and sync/async map — that doc is the highest-leverage artifact to copy structurally. 7) For the why-Gleam vs why-Elixir axis specifically: geex loses pollux's compile-time Request(r,n)/Result-XOR/exhaustive-Notification guarantees and must replace them with a disciplined runtime-validated boundary layer (the cost ADR-001 explicitly assigns to the Elixir alternative).

code_snippets.snippet: The protocol-heavy nature of the project (every layer is JSON-RPC envelopes flowing in and out) is a good fit — type errors at compile time eliminate a class of bugs the runtime-validation path (TS+zod or Elixir+jsonrpc2_spec) only catches at runtime.
code_snippets.why_notable: The single load-bearing sentence of the why-Gleam rationale. It is also a direct statement of exactly what an Elixir port trades away — making it the crux geex must decide on.

code_snippets.snippet: Source contains the comment `// In mcp there are optional fields` — author already considered MCP and handles missing `params` (defaults to empty object, fixing exactly the bug `jsonrpc2_spec` has). ... Result-shaped Response (`Result(t, ErrorObject)` enforces XOR at the type level).
code_snippets.why_notable: Concretely names the Elixir JSON-RPC library bug (jsonrpc2_spec requiring a params key) that a geex Elixir port would inherit and must work around, plus the type-level XOR guarantee it would lose.

code_snippets.snippet: Pool's cache is a coherence concern, not a supervision concern. Supervisors don't notify peers when a child dies. Pool needs its own monitor on each LSP worker to keep the cache from going stale. This is the standard OTP pattern: structure-by-supervision, communication-by-monitoring.
code_snippets.why_notable: The key OTP insight that ports directly to Elixir: supervision restarts, but Process.monitor + DOWN handling is what keeps the pool cache coherent. geex must implement both layers.

code_snippets.snippet:
session.with_session_and_retry -> pool.get : SYNC actor.call (#9) | Caller blocks until SpawnCompleted from spawner (or cache hit). Pool's HANDLER returns fast since M14; only the caller is blocked.
pool actor -> spawner process : async (process.spawn_unlinked) | M14 refactor. Pool actor doesn't block.
code_snippets.why_notable: The exact post-M14 concurrency fix: the pool GenServer must never block on cold-start; spawning runs in a detached process. This is the highest-value pattern for geex to copy and the one most easily gotten wrong.

code_snippets.snippet: Auto-gen tools take their params and results as `Dynamic` JSON values — there is no Gleam record describing a `HoverParams` or `RenameParams`... ADR-001's whole rationale for choosing Gleam was compile-time enforcement of protocol shapes. Auto-gen abandons that for the tool surface — exactly the layer where shape matters most.
code_snippets.why_notable: Ties the tool-surface design directly back to the type-safety thesis: hand-curated typed tools are the payoff of choosing Gleam. An Elixir port that auto-gens tools would forfeit the project's central bet at its most important layer.

synthesis.executive_summary: pharos-mcp is a production Gleam/BEAM MCP server that bridges LLMs to LSP servers; it parses one NDJSON line into a typed DispatchResult via a single pure handle_line/2, serves that core over interchangeable stdio + Streamable-HTTP transports, and hand-writes ~3000 lines of per-tool JSON Schemas and argument decoders. For geex, the headline takeaway is that pharos has already solved every protocol-and-runtime problem geex's MCP server will hit (envelope handling, stdout cleanliness under a release runtime, supervision shape, cancellation), and those solutions port cleanly to Elixir/OTP — geex already has the right primitives (DynamicSupervisor, Registry, GenServers, built-in JSON in Elixir 1.18). The one place pharos is the anti-pattern rather than the pattern is the tool layer: pharos duplicates each tool's name across four string-keyed tables and hand-syncs schema+decoder+handler, which is exactly the boilerplate geex's macro DSL + commands-as-data design eliminates by deriving the MCP tool from the same %Command{} declaration the minibuffer uses. My strong recommendation is to write geex's MCP server in Elixir (not Gleam): the commands, the registry, the dispatcher, the undo history, and the macro that emits the JSON schema all live in Elixir, and putting the protocol boundary in another language would force a foreign-function trip across the very seam where types are cheapest to maintain in Elixir (a struct + a generated schema). Reserve Gleam for the eventual third-party extension API surface, per notes.md, where it actually earns its keep.

port_directly.item: The pure-core / thin-transport seam: one entry point handle_line(state, raw_line) -> {:reply, json} | :noreply | {:protocol_error, json}, with every transport a ~5-line adapter that maps the tagged result onto its wire.
port_directly.source: server.gleam handle_line/2 + DispatchResult (Reply|NoReply|ProtocolError); http.dispatch maps to 200/204; stdio_worker.dispatch_line maps to stdout writes.
port_directly.why: This is the single highest-value, most directly portable idea. It makes the protocol logic a pure function that geex can unit-test with plain strings, and keeps stdio-vs-anything-else a trivial adapter. In Elixir it becomes a 3-clause case in each transport; geex should adopt the exact three outcomes because the no-reply case (notifications produce NO output) and the protocol-error case (malformed input still needs an error frame) are both load-bearing JSON-RPC truths.

port_directly.item: stdout-cleanliness + unbuffered-flush mechanism for the stdio transport: reserve stdout exclusively for JSON-RPC frames, send ALL logs to stderr, and write each frame via a raw fd-1 port (open {fd,1,1} :binary, port_command Body++\n, port_close to force a synchronous flush) rather than IO.puts.
port_directly.source: pharos_stdin_ffi.erl write_line/1 and the {fd,0,0} line-mode stdin port; the gotcha that Burrito's -noshell :user group leader buffers stdout until stdin EOF and would hang initialize past the host's 30s timeout.
port_directly.why: This is BEAM-runtime knowledge, not Gleam-specific — it transfers verbatim to Elixir Ports. geex WILL hit this exact bug the moment it ships a Burrito-packaged binary (already on the v0.4 roadmap) and an MCP host holds stdin open waiting for the initialize reply. Knowing the fix up front saves a multi-hour debugging session. Use Port.open({:fd, 0, 0}, [...]) for input and the close-per-write raw fd-1 port for output; never route frames through Logger or IO.

port_directly.item: JSON-RPC envelope conventions: id is string-or-int and must be echoed back with its original type; parse errors reply with id null and code -32700; method-not-found -32601; invalid-params -32602; notifications (no id) never get a response.
port_directly.source: server.gleam message_decoder (request-vs-notification by presence of id), id_decoder one_of(int,string), success_response/error_response, dispatch error codes.
port_directly.why: These are spec invariants geex must get exactly right and pharos has them correct. Port the conventions directly: classify request-vs-notification purely on whether the decoded map has an "id" key; preserve id type on the way out; reserve JSON-RPC error objects for protocol faults only.

port_directly.item: Tool-result contract: tool outcomes ride a JSON-RPC SUCCESS whose result is {content: [block], isError: bool}; tool-domain failures set isError:true (NOT a JSON-RPC error). Only parse/method/param faults use the JSON-RPC error object.
port_directly.source: server.gleam tool_text_result/2 and the handle_* wrappers; content_block.gleam Text variant -> {type:"text", text:...}.
port_directly.why: This separation is correct per MCP and a common place to get it wrong. For geex a command that fails at runtime (bad range, read-only buffer) must come back as a successful tool call with isError:true and a human-readable message in a text block, while only a malformed tools/call params object escalates to -32602. Port this rule and the {content:[...], isError} shape verbatim.

port_directly.item: Supervision shape: a root supervisor over subtrees, a DynamicSupervisor for per-resource children, monitor-not-link for cache/coherence (structure-by-supervision, communication-by-monitoring), transient leaf for the stdio worker (EOF => clean stop, crash => restart), and a single-writer process funneling all stdout so concurrent producers can't interleave a half-frame.
port_directly.source: supervisor.gleam (OneForOne root + RestForOne subtrees + transient stdio_worker), pool.gleam monitor-on-DOWN cache eviction, stdio_worker single-writer funnel, ADR-013.
port_directly.why: geex already has this skeleton (Geex.BufferSupervisor is a DynamicSupervisor, Geex.Registry exists, TerminalIO is already the sole owner/writer of prim_tty). The MCP server slots in as one more supervised subtree under Geex.Supervisor. The single-writer-funnel insight directly validates geex's existing TerminalIO design and should be reused for the MCP stdout writer: one GenServer owns the frame stream, dispatchers send it completed frames.

adapt.item: The tool registry and tools/list generation. pharos hand-writes {name, description, inputSchema} JSON per tool in a *_tool_definition() builder, hand-writes a parallel decode_*_arguments decoder, hand-writes a handle_* wrapper, and registers the bare string name in FOUR places (definition body, allowed_tool_definitions pair, dispatch_tool_call case, registry.gleam category). geex inverts this: ONE %Command{} declaration (the macro DSL block) is the single source of truth, and the MCP tool definition, the argument parser/validator, the human help text, and the registry entry are all DERIVED from it.
adapt.source: server.gleam allowed_tool_definitions/0, hover_tool_definition/0, find_references_tool_definition/0, decode_find_references_arguments/0, handle_hover/3; registry.gleam is_allowed/1; ADR-006 curated-typed-tools.
adapt.how: Treat pharos's hand-written shapes as the TARGET OUTPUT of geex's macro, not the authoring model. The macro already plans to emit name/args/types/description/json_schema (notes.md lines 238-246). Add two more derivations from the same arg list: (1) tools/list — Geex.CommandRegistry.all() |> Enum.map to {name, description, inputSchema: json_schema}; this is the macro-free loop notes.md already sketches at lines 264-283. (2) tools/call — Geex.CommandRegistry.lookup(name) -> cmd.parse(arguments) -> %Command{} struct -> Geex.Dispatch.run(struct), wrapping the result in {content:[text], isError}. The arg DSL (arg :range, :coord_range, ...) should generate the JSON Schema property AND the param decoder/validator together, so they cannot drift — fixing pharos's #1 documented gotcha (schema and decoder are independently hand-synced and silently drift). Map each geex arg :type to a JSON Schema type: :coord_range/:atom/:string -> string (with a description telling the LLM the syntax like 'a1-g3'), :integer -> integer, defaults -> omit from required[] and document the default in the property description. The key boundary difference: in pharos the tool name appears 4 times and a typo silently breaks list/call/filter consistency at runtime; in geex the name appears once (in command :copy) and the registry, schema, parser, and dispatcher all key off the same generated struct module.

adapt.item: Two-stage decode of tools/call params. pharos keeps arguments as opaque Dynamic until the tool name is known, then runs the per-tool decoder.
adapt.source: server.gleam decode_tool_call/1 ({name, arguments:Option(Dynamic)}) then per-tool decoder; tool_text_result for results.
adapt.how: Mirror this: parse the outer {name, arguments} envelope generically (built-in JSON.decode in Elixir 1.18 yields a map), then hand the raw arguments map to the command's generated parse/1. geex's advantage is that parse/1 already exists as part of the commands-as-data design (the minibuffer also calls it), so the MCP path reuses the SAME parser the human's minibuffer uses — literally the one-vocabulary-one-dispatcher payoff. Validation failure in parse/1 becomes a -32602; a successful parse yields a %Command{} struct identical to what the minibuffer produces.

adapt.item: initialize handshake result and capabilities advertisement.
adapt.how: Reproduce the shape but improve two things pharos's findings flag: (1) negotiate protocolVersion against the client's requested version instead of hardcoding and always echoing one constant; (2) since geex's command set can change at runtime (plugins drop in new commands, per notes.md), advertise capabilities.tools.listChanged: true and actually emit notifications/tools/list_changed when the command registry changes — pharos sets listChanged:false because its tool set is static, but geex's is not. Use the instructions field to tell the LLM about the grid coordinate vocabulary (a1, a1-g6, a1:g6) so it speaks the same language the human types.

adapt.item: Cancellation via a request registry. pharos registers each in-flight dispatcher pid in an ETS table keyed by JSON-RPC id so notifications/cancelled can send_exit the worker.
adapt.how: Adapt to geex's Registry (already in the tree as Geex.Registry) keyed by JSON-RPC id rather than a bare ETS table. BUT geex's calculus differs: most geex commands are fast, synchronous edits, not 30-90s LSP cold starts. Only commands that fan out to pharos (LSP) are slow. So make cancellation OPTIONAL for v0.5 — run each tools/call in its own Task, register the Task pid by id, and handle notifications/cancelled by killing it; if that's too much for v0.5, dispatch inline and make notifications/cancelled a logged no-op (pharos itself does exactly this no-op on its HTTP transport). The async-per-request + single-writer pattern still applies so a slow LSP-backed command doesn't block the stdin reader.

skip.item: All LSP-specific machinery: the warm-LSP Pool actor, per-(language,workspace) cache, off-actor spawn workers with inflight waitlists, the per-LSP proc GenServer owning an OS Port, $/progress draining, readiness probes, the lsp_request_raw escape hatch, capability gating, and the 15-row layered timeout model.
skip.why: geex does NOT re-implement any of this — it CONSUMES pharos as a subprocess (notes.md 'Pharos-mcp reuse': MCP client over stdio). geex's MCP server EXPOSES editor commands; it does not front language servers. The entire pool/spawn/readiness/timeout subsystem is solving pharos's domain problem (managing N language-server subprocesses), which is orthogonal to exposing a command registry. geex will eventually be an MCP CLIENT of pharos and an MCP SERVER of its own commands — two different roles. Skip the server-side LSP plumbing entirely.

skip.item: HTTP / Streamable-HTTP transport, SSE channel, Mcp-Session-Id sessions, origin/DNS-rebind validation, port-file discovery, the sessions GenServer, and the /mcp/respond + SSE server-request push (which are stubbed in pharos anyway).
skip.why: For v0.5 the only client is an LLM agent living in a geex pane (or an external claude-code) connecting over stdio to the editor process. There is no remote/multi-client requirement yet, and notes.md explicitly scopes the AI loop to a local pane. stdio is sufficient and simplest. The pure-core seam means HTTP can be added later as a second adapter without touching the dispatch logic — so dropping it now costs nothing future. pharos's own HTTP path is second-class (no cancel registry, half-wired SSE), reinforcing that it's not worth porting until a remote-collaboration story actually exists (which notes.md flags as a different product).

skip.item: The pollux dependency / ADR-002 'use a typed JSON-RPC library' decision, and any attempt to find a typed JSON-RPC lib for Elixir.
skip.why: The findings reveal pollux is declared but NOT actually imported anywhere in pharos src/ — pharos hand-rolls its own envelope shapes. So 'use pollux' is not even what pharos really did. For geex, the JSON-RPC envelope is tiny (a handful of fields) and Elixir 1.18 ships a built-in JSON module — adding a JSON-RPC framework dependency is over-engineering. Hand-roll the ~80-line envelope encoder/decoder. ADR-002's survey of buggy Elixir JSON-RPC libs (jsonrpc2_spec's optional-params bug, no Notification type) is a reason to AVOID those libs, not to seek one.

skip.item: Burrito meta-flags / dual entry points / --doctor / --purge-cache / warm subcommand / config precedence chain (TOML < env), and the per-instance orphan-tracking cleanup.
skip.why: These solve pharos's standalone-binary distribution and LSP-orphan-reaping problems. geex's MCP server is an in-process subtree of an already-running editor, not a separately-launched binary with its own CLI surface and config files. geex boots the MCP server from Geex.Application when AI integration is enabled; there is no separate process to warm, no language config to layer, no orphan LSPs to reap (pharos manages those). Skip the entire entry-point/config/cleanup apparatus.

gleam_vs_elixir_decision.recommendation: Write geex's MCP boundary in ELIXIR, not Gleam. This is the opinionated call. The decisive argument is the location of the source of truth: geex's entire value proposition is that ONE Elixir macro declaration (command :copy do ... end) generates the struct, the runner, the help text, the registry entry, AND the JSON schema — and the LLM uses the SAME Elixir dispatcher (Geex.Dispatch.run/1) and the SAME parse/1 the human's minibuffer uses, landing in the SAME undo history. The MCP server's job is almost entirely 'take the JSON schema the macro already produced, list it; take the params, call the same parser, run the same dispatcher.' That logic is a thin, mostly-glue layer sitting directly on top of Elixir data structures (a %Command{} struct, a registry map, a generated JSON-schema map). Putting it in Gleam would force a language boundary across the one seam where it hurts most: the schema is generated by an Elixir macro at Elixir compile time, the registry is an Elixir process/ETS table, the dispatcher and undo history are Elixir, the commands themselves are Elixir. A Gleam MCP layer would have to receive Elixir-generated schemas as opaque dynamic terms, marshal params back into Elixir, and call Elixir dispatch via FFI — re-introducing exactly the untyped boundary Gleam was supposed to remove, plus a build-system and ABI seam, for a protocol envelope that is about 80 lines of trivial JSON. notes.md reserves Gleam for 'the extension API surface' — the contract third-party EXTENSION authors plug into — which is a genuinely different, genuinely typed-contract-shaped boundary. The MCP server is not that; it is an internal adapter over geex's own command system. Use Gleam where notes.md plans (extension API), keep MCP in Elixir.
gleam_vs_elixir_decision.tradeoffs: What you give up by choosing Elixir is exactly what pharos's findings document Gleam buys: compile-time exhaustiveness on the request/notification split, a sum type making result-XOR-error unrepresentable, and a decoder that turns malformed input into a typed Result rather than a runtime crash. You must re-acquire those guarantees at runtime: (1) classify request-vs-notification with an explicit Map.has_key?(msg, "id") guard and a with-pipeline that funnels any JSON.decode failure to a -32700/-32602 frame instead of letting it raise; (2) write the dispatch as a case on method with an explicit catch-all -> -32601 (the compiler will NOT warn you if you forget a method); (3) cover the envelope with property tests and typespecs/Dialyzer rather than the compiler. This is real but small and bounded — the envelope is tiny and stable, and the macro recovers MOST of the safety Gleam's compiler would give, because the schema, parser, and handler are all GENERATED from one arg-list declaration (geex structurally CANNOT have pharos's #1 bug of schema/decoder/handler drift, since they come from one source). A hybrid (Gleam only for the envelope decode/encode, Elixir for everything else) is possible but NOT worth it: it adds a Gleam build target and an FFI hop to type-check ~6 fields, while the interesting typing (the per-command arg shapes) lives on the Elixir side and is already protected by the macro. Recommendation stands: Elixir for the MCP server, Gleam deferred to the extension API where the contract is with external untrusted authors and the typed boundary is the actual product feature.

synthesis.mcp_spec_notes:
PROTOCOL VERSION: pharos hardcodes "2024-11-05" and echoes it back regardless of what the client requested. For geex, accept the client's requested protocolVersion from initialize params and either echo it back if supported or reply with the highest version geex supports; do NOT blindly hardcode. As of early 2026 the current MCP revision is the 2025-06-18 line (the 2025-03-26 revision removed JSON-RPC batching, which neither geex nor pharos needs). Pick the version geex actually implements, store it as a module attribute, and negotiate against the client's value.

TRANSPORT: stdio transport is newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) — one JSON-RPC message per \n, NO Content-Length framing (that's LSP, not MCP). One message per line, stdout reserved exclusively for frames, logs to stderr. This is the only transport geex needs for v0.5.

MESSAGE CLASSIFICATION: a JSON-RPC message with an "id" is a request (gets a response); without an "id" it is a notification (gets NO response, ever). id is string-or-number and must be echoed with original type. Validate this structurally.

METHODS geex must implement: initialize (handshake), notifications/initialized (ack, no reply), tools/list, tools/call, ping (return {} — pharos OMITS this and a ping gets -32601, which is a compliance gap geex should NOT replicate; add an explicit ping handler returning an empty result), and notifications/cancelled (no reply; cancel or no-op).

ERROR CODES: -32700 parse error (id null), -32600 invalid request, -32601 method not found, -32602 invalid params, -32603 internal error. pharos uses -32700/-32601/-32602 only. geex should also emit -32603 for unexpected internal failures and SHOULD support the optional error.data field for structured payloads — pharos's error_response emits only code+message and omits data; adding data lets geex attach structured validation errors from the command parser.

CONTENT BLOCKS: tool results are {content: [block...], isError: bool}. A text block is {type:"text", text:"..."}. The spec also defines image ({type:"image", data, mimeType}) and resource ({type:"resource", resource:{...}}) blocks. pharos implements text only and notes the others as future. geex needs only text for v0.5 (commands return status/diffs as text), but model the content block as a tagged type/struct so image/resource can be added later without reshaping the result encoder. Tool-level failures = isError:true in a SUCCESS response; only protocol faults use the JSON-RPC error object.

CAPABILITIES: initialize result advertises capabilities. Because geex commands can be added at runtime (plugins), advertise {tools:{listChanged:true}} and actually send notifications/tools/list_changed when the registry changes — unlike pharos which is static (listChanged:false).

open_decisions.question: Is the geex MCP server written in Elixir or Gleam?
open_decisions.options: Elixir (consistent with the command system, macro-generated schemas, dispatcher, and undo history all being Elixir) vs Gleam (consistent with notes.md's 'Gleam for the extension API surface' and pharos's compile-time-protocol-safety precedent) vs hybrid (Gleam envelope codec, Elixir everything else).
open_decisions.recommendation: Elixir. The source of truth (commands, macro-generated schema, dispatcher, undo) is all Elixir; the MCP server is a thin adapter over it; a Gleam boundary here re-introduces an FFI/untyped hop at the worst seam. Reserve Gleam for the third-party extension API per notes.md, which is a genuinely different typed-contract boundary.

open_decisions.question: Does v0.5 ship request cancellation, or dispatch inline?
open_decisions.options: (a) Run each tools/call in a Task registered by JSON-RPC id in Geex.Registry, kill on notifications/cancelled (matches pharos stdio). (b) Dispatch inline on the reader process and treat notifications/cancelled as a logged no-op (matches pharos HTTP).
open_decisions.recommendation: Start with async-per-request Tasks (so a slow pharos-backed command can't block the stdin reader and so the single-writer funnel applies) but make the cancel-by-kill itself optional — wire the registry now, implement send_exit later. Most geex commands are fast synchronous edits; only LSP-fanout commands are slow.

open_decisions.question: How do macro arg types map to JSON Schema, and where does the LLM learn the grid coordinate grammar?
open_decisions.options: Map :coord_range/:atom/:string -> JSON 'string' with a descriptive 'description' carrying the syntax; :integer -> 'integer'; defaulted args omitted from required[]. Teach the grammar via per-arg descriptions, the initialize 'instructions' field, or a dedicated grid-syntax skill/resource.
open_decisions.recommendation: Put the syntax (a1, a1-g6, a1:g6, multi-selection) in BOTH the arg description (so it rides every relevant tool schema) AND the initialize instructions field (so the model has it globally). Keep a single arg-type -> schema mapping table in the macro so adding a new arg type is one edit.

open_decisions.question: Where does the MCP server sit in the supervision tree, and is it always-on or feature-gated?
open_decisions.options: Always start it under Geex.Supervisor vs gate it behind a config flag (like the existing :start_terminal pattern in Geex.Application) vs start it on-demand when an AI pane opens.
open_decisions.recommendation: Feature-gate it exactly like the existing terminal_io_child/0 pattern (Application.get_env(:geex, :start_mcp, ...)). The AI loop is explicitly v0.5+, so default-off until then; when on, it's a supervised subtree (a stdio transport GenServer + a single-writer frame GenServer + an optional request Task supervisor).

open_decisions.question: How is the command registry populated and does tools/list reflect runtime changes?
open_decisions.options: Aggregate at compile time via module attributes (static, fast) vs an ETS/Registry table populated at boot and mutated when plugins load (dynamic, supports listChanged) vs both (compile-time core + runtime plugin additions).
open_decisions.recommendation: Both: macro registers core commands at compile time into a central table that plugins also write to at load time (plugins are Code.compile_file'd Elixir modules per notes.md). Advertise tools.listChanged:true and emit notifications/tools/list_changed when a plugin adds commands — this is the one place geex genuinely diverges from pharos's static tool set.

open_decisions.question: What is geex's relationship to pharos at the MCP layer — does geex re-expose pharos's LSP tools, proxy them, or just consume them internally?
open_decisions.options: (a) geex is purely an MCP server of its own commands; the editor brain is a separate MCP client of pharos. (b) geex also proxies/forwards pharos's LSP tools through its own MCP server so an external agent sees one unified tool surface (notes.md line 341 'Pharos-mcp's LSP tools (forwarded or proxied)').
open_decisions.recommendation: Defer (b). For v0.5 ship (a): geex exposes editor commands; the editor brain and any agent talk to pharos directly as a separate MCP server. Proxying adds a client+server bridge inside geex with no clear v0.5 payoff; revisit when 'one unified tool surface for external agents' becomes a real requirement.

synthesis.recommended_geex_shape:
Target layout under lib/geex/mcp/ (all Elixir), slotting into the existing Geex.Application tree alongside TerminalIO/Renderer/Session/BufferSupervisor:

- Geex.MCP.Protocol (pure module, no process): the heart, ported from pharos's handle_line/2. handle_line(line :: String.t()) :: {:reply, iodata} | :noreply | {:protocol_error, iodata}. Internally: JSON.decode/1 (built-in, Elixir 1.18) -> on error {:protocol_error, error_frame(nil, -32700, "Parse error")}; on success classify by Map.has_key?(msg, "id"). Request -> dispatch by method; notification -> :noreply. Holds encode helpers success_frame(id, result) / error_frame(id, code, message, data \\ nil) that build {jsonrpc:"2.0", id, result|error}, preserving id type. This module is pure and fully unit-testable with string fixtures — copy pharos's test discipline here.

- Geex.MCP.Dispatch (inside Protocol or a sibling): case on method — "initialize" -> negotiated handshake result; "tools/list" -> tools_list(); "tools/call" -> tool_call(params); "ping" -> {}; catch-all -> -32601. tools_list/0 is the notes.md sketch: Geex.CommandRegistry.all() |> Enum.map(fn cmd -> %{name: cmd.name, description: cmd.description, inputSchema: cmd.json_schema} end) wrapped as %{tools: [...]}. tool_call/1 = Geex.CommandRegistry.lookup(name) -> cmd.parse(arguments) (the SAME parser the minibuffer uses) -> on {:error, why} return -32602; on {:ok, %Command{}=struct} -> Geex.Dispatch.run(struct) (the SAME dispatcher humans hit, landing in the SAME undo history) -> wrap as %{content:[%{type:"text", text: render(result)}], isError: failed?}.

- HOW A %Command{} BECOMES A TOOL (the macro seam): the existing/planned Geex.Command macro (notes.md lines 220-246) already emits the struct + runner + help + json_schema. Extend its arg DSL so each arg :name, :type, opts entry generates, from ONE declaration: (1) a JSON Schema property (type-mapped: :coord_range/:atom/:string->"string" with a syntax description, :integer->"integer"), included in required[] unless it has a default; (2) a clause in the generated parse/1 that reads and validates that field; (3) the struct field. This is the inversion of pharos's bug: schema + parser + struct cannot drift because they share one source. CommandRegistry is populated at compile time by the macro and is also writable at plugin-load time.

- Geex.MCP.StdioTransport (GenServer): owns the input side. On init, Port.open({:fd, 0, 0}, [:binary, :eof, {:line, 65535}]) (the pharos {fd,0,0} line-mode trick to dodge :user buffering). handle_info for {port, {:data, {:eol, line}}} -> spawn/Task a dispatcher that calls Geex.MCP.Protocol.handle_line(line) and sends the result to the writer; register the Task pid by JSON-RPC id in Geex.Registry for cancellation; {port,:eof} -> graceful stop. Reader never blocks so notifications/cancelled arrive promptly.

- Geex.MCP.Writer (GenServer): the single-writer funnel (same role TerminalIO already plays for prim_tty). All frames go through here; it writes each via a raw fd-1 port (Port.open({:fd,1,1},[:binary]), command(port, [frame, "\n"]), close to force synchronous flush) — the pharos write_line mechanism, verbatim, so initialize doesn't hang under a Burrito release. Guarantees frame atomicity across concurrent dispatchers.

- Supervision: add an Geex.MCP.Supervisor subtree to Geex.Application.start/2, feature-gated like terminal_io_child/0 (Application.get_env(:geex, :start_mcp, false) until v0.5). It supervises Writer, StdioTransport, and (optionally) a Task.Supervisor for per-request dispatchers. Transient/clean-exit semantics on the transport: stdin EOF = normal stop, crash = restart. Reuses the existing Geex.Registry for request-id -> Task-pid cancellation. No LSP pool, no HTTP, no sessions, no config-precedence machinery.

Net: ~5 small modules. The only non-trivial code is the macro's arg-list -> {schema, parser, struct} expansion (which geex is building anyway for the minibuffer) and the two Port FFI details (stdin line-mode port, fd-1 close-per-write). Everything else is the pharos seam translated 1:1 into Elixir.
